      features/                 # install, update, uninstall, status, namespace, recover, vap-access-control
      suite_test.go             # entrypoint: shared runner + shared steps + OC-specific steps
    catalogd/
      features/                 # ha, proxy, tls
      suite_test.go
    object-controller/
      features/                 # revision, user-managed-fields
      suite_test.go
    platform/                   # cross-component features
      features/                 # metrics (OC + catalogd), demos
      suite_test.go

Each */suite_test.go is a thin Go test package that calls the shared runner, pointing it at its own features/ directory and registering the shared step set plus any component-specific steps.

docs.title: How "run one" and "run all" work
docs.text:
• Run all: Go's ... wildcard (go test ./test/e2e/...) discovers and runs every component subpackage automatically — no central list to maintain. The canonical run-all stays the make test-e2e target, which already carries the established invocation: -count=1 (test caching off, so every run actually contacts the cluster) and the two-pass tag policy — ~@Serial && ~@demo concurrently, then @Serial && ~@demo serially, with @demo run only by update-demos.yaml.
  • Run one component: go test ./test/e2e/catalogd/... (etc.), carrying the same -count=1 and --godog.tags flags as the run-all invocation.
  • Existing tag-based selection (@Serial serial vs. concurrent, ~@demo exclusion) is preserved within each suite via --godog.tags.

docs.title: Why this over the alternatives
docs.text:
• Tag-only on a single suite (rejected): smallest change, but leaves everything in one package/dir — it does not create the clean boundary a repo split needs, and features are not physically owned. Weakest match to the driver.
  • Hybrid single parameterized runner (rejected): physically separates features/steps but keeps one runner selected by flag. The runner becomes a shared choke point that accretes if component == … conditionals the moment components need different suite-level behavior, and the conversion to per-entrypoint has to happen at split time anyway. We pay the cost later without the clean boundary now.

The expensive work — partitioning features and (eventually) factoring the step library — is identical across these options. Approach A gives each component its own entrypoint without adding component conditionals to the shared runner. Helpers remain internal until a repository split requires an explicit library boundary.

docs.title: Cross-Cutting Feature Ownership
docs.text:
Some features are not cleanly owned by a single component. Assignment is by the primary user-facing API under test, with a dedicated platform/ bucket for genuinely cross-component features.

Feature Owner Notes install, update, uninstall, status, namespace, recover, vap-access-control operator-controller Exercise ClusterExtension; catalogd is an assumed dependency, not the subject. revision, user-managed-fields object-controller Already @BoxcutterRuntime. ha, proxy, tls catalogd tls.feature comments confirm all scenarios test catalogd only. All @Serial. metrics platform Single scenario outline tests both operator-controller and catalogd via an Examples table. Splitting would duplicate the scenario; keep as one cross-component feature. demos platform @demo, cross-cutting, already excluded from normal runs via ~@demo. Governed by update-demos.yaml.

Decision: Introduce a platform/ suite for cross-component features rather than forcing metrics/demos into a single owner. The "run all" target (go test ./test/e2e/...) covers it automatically. This is the one design choice most worth confirming on review; the alternative (split metrics per component, drop platform/) is viable but duplicates the metrics scenario.

docs.title: The Shared Library Boundary
docs.text:
test/internal/e2e holds the runner and test utilities shared by the component and upgrade suites. Go's internal visibility lets packages under test/ reuse them without treating exported test functions and types as public Go APIs. Component-specific step packages also stay under this internal tree when they are separated in PR3.

  • World/state + hooks (hooks.go): scenario setup/teardown, namespace lifecycle.
  • Common Given steps: "OLM is available", "an image registry is available", "a catalog … with packages", generic apply/assert helpers. These are prerequisites every component needs.
  • Runner boilerplate: the Godog Options, the --e2e.scenario prefix filter (findScenarioFirstLineNumberByPrefix), and summary wiring (test/internal/summary) — currently inlined in features_test.go:36-134. Lifted into a shared helper so each suite_test.go is a few lines. Summary templates are embedded so generation works from any suite directory.
  • Diagnostics: support-bundle.yaml.

test/upgrade-e2e already imports test/e2e/steps; after the move it becomes another consumer of test/internal/e2e/steps. Envtest helpers used outside test/ move from test/utils.go to internal/testutil, where API and controller unit tests can import them.

A future repository split must extract or copy the required internal helpers with the suites. These helpers do not provide a cross-repository compatibility guarantee. Moving the existing public packages still reports API removals during this migration; the initial transition requires maintainer review and the existing go-apidiff-override label. Subsequent internal-helper changes should no longer need that override.

docs.title: PR Sequence
docs.text: The ordering is deliberate: PR2 is safe precisely because PR3 has not happened yet. Through PR1–PR2 the step definitions remain one monolithic package, so every component suite can register the entire shared step set. A feature moved into catalogd/features/ still resolves all its steps. Godog Strict: true fails only on undefined/pending steps, never on registered-but-unused ones, so over-registering is free. The step split (PR3) therefore blocks nothing.

docs.title: PR1 — Reroot layout + establish internal helpers (mechanical, behavior-preserving)
docs.text:
• git mv test/e2e/features/ → test/e2e/operator-controller/features/ (all features stay together for now).
  • git mv test/e2e/steps/ → test/internal/e2e/steps/.
  • Lift runner boilerplate (TestMain, --e2e.scenario filter, summary wiring) from features_test.go into test/internal/e2e so later suites reuse it.
  • Create the operator-controller suite_test.go calling the shared runner.
  • Reserve catalogd/features/, object-controller/features/, and platform/features/ with .gitkeep files. Their suite entry points and feature moves follow in PR2.
  • Move support-bundle.yaml into test/internal/e2e/.
  • Keep summary generation under test/internal/summary and embed its templates.
  • Move test/utils.go to internal/testutil and update unit-test imports and project-root discovery.
  • Update all references in the same PR:
  • test/upgrade-e2e/upgrade_test.go import path for the steps package.
  • Makefile targets referencing ./test/e2e/features_test.go (lines ~431, 435, 446, 479, 740) and the e2e/% scenario path.
  • .github/workflows/update-demos.yaml paths (features/demos.feature, steps/demo_steps.go, steps/asciicast_*.go) and the support-bundle.yaml path in e2e.yaml:72.
  • Constraint: no behavior change. The suite still runs the same scenarios; only locations and import paths move.
  • ⚠️ CI workflow edits require maintainer sign-off (per AGENTS.md "never modify .github/workflows/* without explicit permission"). Flag this explicitly in the PR; the demos/support-bundle path updates are unavoidable consequences of the move.

docs.title: PR2 — Sort features into component suites (may split per component)
docs.text:
• Add a thin suite_test.go in each reserved catalogd/, object-controller/, and platform/ directory, calling the shared runner and registering the full shared step set. Remove each .gitkeep when populating its feature directory.
  • git mv features to their owners per the ownership table. Moving demos.feature into platform/features/ shifts a path tracked by .github/workflows/update-demos.yaml; update that workflow in the same PR (maintainer sign-off, as in PR1).
  • The operator-controller suite shrinks as features leave; go test ./test/e2e/... now runs four suites.
  • Can be landed as separate PRs per component (e.g. object-controller first, then catalogd, then platform).
  • Still no step refactor — every suite registers everything, so all steps resolve.

docs.title: PR3 — Split the step library per component (judgment-heavy, incremental)
docs.text:
• Partition test/internal/e2e/steps into truly-shared vs. component-specific packages under test/internal/e2e. Rough starting map:
  • Shared: hooks.go, world setup, "OLM is available"/registry/catalog Given steps, generic apply/assert (the shared portion of steps.go).
  • operator-controller: ClusterExtension-specific steps from steps.go.
  • catalogd: ha_steps.go, proxy_steps.go, tls_steps.go.
  • platform/demos: demo_steps.go, asciicast_hooks.go, asciicast_recorder.go.
  • upgrade-e2e: upgrade_steps.go (consider relocating to the upgrade suite).
  • Moving the demo step files (demo_steps.go, asciicast_*.go) again shifts paths tracked by .github/workflows/update-demos.yaml; update that workflow in the same PR.
  • Each suite registers shared + its own steps.
  • Can land one component at a time; nothing depends on it completing. A future repo split can then select the required internal helpers explicitly.

docs.title: Sequencing summary
docs.text: PR Scope Risk Splittable PR1 Reroot + internal helpers, update refs Low (mechanical) No PR2 Sort features into suites Low (moves; over-registered steps) Up to 3–4 PRs PR3 Split step library Medium (judgment) Up to 3–4 PRs, incremental

docs.title: Testing & Verification
docs.text:
• Each PR: make test-e2e (and make test-experimental-e2e for object-controller / @BoxcutterRuntime features) must stay green. Because PR1–PR2 are behavior-preserving moves, the same scenario set runs with the same pass/fail.
  • Run-all: verify go test ./test/e2e/... discovers and runs every component suite.
  • Run-one: verify go test ./test/e2e/<component>/... runs only that component's features.
  • Tag behavior: confirm @Serial scenarios still run serially and ~@demo exclusion still applies within each suite.
  • upgrade-e2e: confirm it still builds and runs after the steps package moves.
  • make verify / make lint for import and formatting correctness.

docs.title: Open Decisions (for review)
docs.text:
1. platform/ bucket vs. splitting metrics/demos per component. Recommended: keep platform/. Alternative: duplicate the metrics scenario outline per component and drop platform/.
  2. Per-component Makefile targets. Whether to add test-e2e-<component> convenience targets, or rely on go test ./test/e2e/<component>/... directly. (Leaning: add thin targets mirroring the existing test-e2e env setup, since cluster/manifest env wiring is non-trivial.)
  3. upgrade_steps.go home. Relocate into the upgrade suite during PR3, or keep in test/internal/e2e/steps.

docs.title: ClusterObjectDeployment contract
docs.text:
ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) is a mutable orchestration resource that creates ClusterObjectSet (COS) snapshots and observes their rollout. This proposal defines the template, revision lifecycle, and status contract for COD and COS.

The design was prototyped in orb-operator.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
COD owns revision creation, template metadata propagation, and rollout status. COS owns phased application, probes, shared-object ownership handoff, and teardown. Clients update one COD instead of allocating revision numbers themselves.

Group membership and controller ownership answer different questions. All COSs with the same immutable spec.group are revision-chain members. COD manages only COSs controlled by its UID or legitimately adopted from an ownerless state. Revision allocation considers the whole group; COD health and revision summaries use its owned subset. A foreign controller reference is not replaced.

Solid arrows show reconciliation and application; dotted arrows show status feedback.

flowchart TD
    client["Client"] -->|updates template| cod["ClusterObjectDeployment<br/>Mutable desired state"]
    cod -->|reconciled by| codController["COD controller"]
    codController -->|creates and owns snapshots| cos["ClusterObjectSet revisions"]
    cos -->|reconciled by| cosController["COS controller"]
    cosController -->|"applies phases, runs probes,<br/>hands off ownership and tears down"| objects["Managed Kubernetes objects"]
    cosController -.->|updates rollout status| cos
    cos -.->|"conditions, completion timestamps<br/>and object counts"| codController
    codController -.->|"Available, Progressing,<br/>activeRevisions and objectCounts"| cod

docs.title: Desired API
docs.text:
The resource is cluster-scoped, has short name cod, and uses olm.operatorframework.io/v1. Its status is updated through the status subresource. The outer spec and template remain mutable.

Field Proposed contract spec.progressDeadlineMinutes Optional *int32; minimum 1 when supplied. Omitted means no deadline. Explicit 0 is invalid. It belongs to COD, outside the revision template. spec.template Required template with bounded metadata and a COS content spec. spec.template.metadata.labels Optional map of at most 32 Kubernetes-valid labels, copied onto each COS. spec.template.metadata.annotations Optional map of at most 32 Kubernetes-valid annotations, copied onto each COS. spec.template.spec.collisionProtection Optional enum: Prevent, IfNoController, or None. Omitted has effective value Prevent, which COD writes explicitly into COS's required field. spec.template.spec.phases Required ordered list of 1–20 uniquely named ClusterObjectSetPhase entries. Reuse the existing phase/object validation, including the 50-object phase limit. spec.template.spec.progressionProbes Optional []ProgressionProbe with the existing selector/assertion types and validation. Preserve the current COS probe API until its separate redesign.

Reuse the existing COS content types. Objects retain the existing exactly-one-of object/ref representation; references continue pointing to immutable Secret content. COD does not dereference or apply that content. Inline per-object assertions and ClusterObjectSlice references are separate API extensions outside this proposal.

group, revision, and lifecycleState are controller-assigned COS fields and are absent from the template. The legacy COS progressDeadlineMinutes field is also absent from the template: COD's inactivity deadline has different semantics and must not be forwarded into COS. Removing the legacy field is a follow-up change after clients are migrated to COD.

Template metadata applies to the COS resource, not every managed object. To change a managed object's labels or annotations, edit that object in the template content. COD root metadata is not automatically copied. The controller owns olm.operatorframework.io/template-hash; callers cannot supply that key in template labels. Caller metadata is cloned rather than mutated when constructing a child.

Each annotation value is bounded to 256 KiB. The complete copied annotation map must also fit Kubernetes' aggregate 256 KiB annotation budget, including keys and any controller-added annotations. Validation must prevent a template from producing invalid child metadata.

docs.title: Example shape
docs.text:
apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterObjectDeployment
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  progressDeadlineMinutes: 5
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: example
    spec:
      collisionProtection: Prevent
      phases:
        - name: namespaces
          objects:
            - object:
                apiVersion: v1
                kind: Namespace
                metadata:
                  name: example
        - name: resources
          objects:
            - object:
                apiVersion: v1
                kind: ConfigMap
                metadata:
                  name: settings
                  namespace: example
                data:
                  mode: enabled

This describes the proposed API shape, not an installable resource before the COD API PR lands. Optional structs use value types and omitzero; scalar/map fields use the repository's established JSON conventions. The deadline pointer preserves the difference between absence and an invalid explicit zero.

docs.title: Template identity and revision identity
docs.text:
Both template metadata and template spec participate in identity. Root metadata, status, and deadline-only edits do not create a revision. Map key order is irrelevant; changes to phase, object, or probe list order participate in identity.

Identity uses the declared template, before filling controller-assigned COS fields. Omission and an explicitly supplied collisionProtection: Prevent are distinct templates even though their effective collision behavior is equal. Editing between those representations creates a revision. Absent and empty optional maps have the same serialized representation.

A hash identifies candidates; a label match alone does not establish content equality or ownership. Matching and AlreadyExists recovery verify the effective child template and controller UID. The concrete hash encoding is an implementation detail, not a caller-facing promise of collision-free identity.

Each child has spec.group = COD.metadata.name, a positive int64 revision, lifecycleState: Active, and name {group}-{revision}. Its controller reference contains the COD's actual UID. Allocate revision 1 for an empty group, otherwise the maximum existing group revision plus one, including archived or foreign members. Refuse allocation at math.MaxInt64 rather than wrapping. A → B → A creates a new higher revision; an archived COS cannot be reactivated.

COD names follow the proposed COS group's pattern ^[a-z]([a-z0-9-]*[a-z0-9])?$ and 1–52 character limit. The limit ensures COD.name is a valid group. Child names must satisfy the CRD's name validation, using the applicable Kubernetes object-name rules.

docs.title: Observed API
docs.text:
COD status exposes conditions, active revisions, and object counts:

Field Proposed contract status.conditions []metav1.Condition, keyed by type, with Available and Progressing. status.activeRevisions List keyed by COS name, containing the child's current conditions; sorted by increasing revision when written. Includes owned active, non-deleting COSs and a child acknowledged as newly created. status.objectCounts Optional copy of the highest owned active COS's counts: total, present, synced, and available. Omitted if that child has not reported counts or no active child exists.

Counts are not summed across revisions: they may manage overlapping objects. COS status remains the source for phase and object details. No additional rollout record, desired-template hash, or timer-start field is proposed in COD status.

Each COD condition records the generation evaluated by the controller. observedGeneration does not mean the desired content is installed; the condition type and reason supply that meaning. Preserve lastTransitionTime while condition status is unchanged, and avoid identical status writes.

docs.title: Available
docs.text:
Available describes the health of the owned active COSs. Count only owned active COSs that are not being deleted.

Active revisions Available status Reason None False NotAvailable Exactly one, with COS Ready=True True Available Exactly one, with COS Ready absent, False, or Unknown False NotAvailable More than one Unknown Progressing

This is current installation health, not a guarantee that the desired template has completed. If revision A is healthy but creation of B fails, Available remains True while Progressing reports waiting for B, including the creation error. Once B is created, Available becomes Unknown during the transition. After a completed revision becomes unhealthy, Available becomes False without restarting rollout timing.

docs.title: Progressing
docs.text:
Evaluate only the highest owned active revision. A historical matching template or an older completed revision does not complete the current rollout. The selected child must match the current desired template before its progress is used.

Current rollout state Progressing status Reason Matching COS has completedAt set False NewClusterObjectSetProgressed Matching COS is incomplete, deadline disabled or not exceeded True NewClusterObjectSetProgressing No matching COS exists; creation is pending, deadline disabled or not exceeded True NewClusterObjectSetProgressing Matching COS or pending creation has exceeded its deadline False ProgressDeadlineExceeded

Creation failures remain visible in the pending condition message while retries continue. Completion is a historical latch: a matching COS that completed once continues reporting NewClusterObjectSetProgressed after a health regression.

Progressing=True describes unfinished rollout work. Progressing=False describes completion or an exceeded deadline; the reason distinguishes those states.

docs.title: Example revision rollout
docs.text:
This example starts with one healthy owned revision A and changes the template to B. The new revision completes without exceeding a deadline. Controllers reconcile asynchronously, so a reconciliation may observe several changes together.

sequenceDiagram
    participant client as Client
    participant api as Kubernetes API
    participant codController as COD controller
    participant cosController as COS controller
    participant objects as Managed objects

    Note over api,codController: A is the only owned active COS<br/>Available=True
    client->>api: Update COD template to B
    api-->>codController: Observe COD change
    codController->>api: List all COSs in the group
    api-->>codController: Group revisions and ownership
    codController->>codController: Verify no matching highest owned active COS<br/>Allocate max group revision + 1
    codController->>api: Create B snapshot with COD owner UID
    codController->>api: Report Available=Unknown, Progressing=True
    api-->>cosController: Observe new COS

    loop Each phase of B
        cosController->>objects: Apply objects and evaluate probes
        objects-->>cosController: Observed object state
        cosController->>api: Persist phase completedAt and object counts
        api-->>codController: Observe COS status change
        codController->>api: Refresh COD status from owned active COSs
    end

    cosController->>api: Persist B completedAt and Ready=True
    api-->>codController: Observe COS completion
    codController->>api: Report Progressing=False<br/>Reason: NewClusterObjectSetProgressed
    cosController->>api: Archive predecessor A
    api-->>codController: Observe COS lifecycle change
    codController->>api: Report Available=True and only B in activeRevisions

docs.title: Deadline and recovery
docs.text:
With a matching incomplete COS, the milestone is the latest of its creation time and persisted phase completedAt timestamps. A phase completion advances the milestone; polling, error retries, and condition changes do not. Timeout occurs when elapsed time is greater than or equal to the configured interval. Completion is checked first and ends rollout timing even if the deadline previously elapsed.

Without a matching COS, use the persisted Progressing condition to evaluate pending creation:

Previous Progressing observation Pending-creation baseline or result No previous condition COD creation time. Status True Its existing lastTransitionTime, including across template/generation edits. Status False after a completed rollout The time the new pending rollout is first observed; the transition to True persists that time. Reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded and deadline still enabled Remain timed out until a matching COS is created, including across template edits or increases to the deadline.

Successfully creating a matching COS switches to that COS's creation/phase milestones. Restart reconstructs the same evaluation from persisted conditions and COS timestamps. Template edits during an ongoing pending rollout retain the existing condition-based baseline and do not start a fresh creation window.

Deadline-only edits do not stamp a COS. For a matching incomplete COS, evaluate the new interval against its existing milestone. For a pending timed-out rollout, the timeout remains while a deadline is enabled. Removing the deadline must stop reporting ProgressDeadlineExceeded and return an incomplete rollout to Progressing=True. Deadline disablement takes precedence over a previously recorded pending timeout.

A pending creation always retries, since a failed create may produce no child event. With a matching child and a configured unexpired deadline, schedule a wakeup no later than expiry even if no status event arrives. After timeout, retain child watches and reconciliation; actual later phase progress can resume Progressing, and completion ends it. Timeout neither archives children nor automatically rolls back. Arithmetic and requeue calculations must remain safe for every admitted positive int32 deadline value.

docs.title: Alternative: a persisted rollout record
docs.text:
A future contract could store the desired template identity and a rollout start timestamp together in COD status. That would allow a distinct creation window for each new template even when Progressing remains True, and make timer identity independent of condition transition times. Deadline-only edits would retain the same record; a template identity change would start a new one. Actual phase progress would still come from COS timestamps.

This adds API fields and decisions about when the record starts, changes, or is cleared, including recovery after timeout and parent recreation. It would need corresponding restart and partial-write tests. The proposed baseline uses condition timestamps; a persisted record is an alternative for a separate API discussion if independent per-template creation windows are required.

docs.title: Dependencies and review decisions
docs.text:
Related work Contract dependency COS group identity Immutable group and shared group lookup; COD naming follows the group's admission contract. Detailed COS status Persistent phase completion, completion latch, and object counts. Existing phase digests do not indicate phase completion. COS Ready semantics COD reads the child condition type/status, not specific child reason strings. Revision chains and foreign ownership Keep group membership separate from management ownership. Group-only COS sibling behavior and foreign-leading OwnerConflict handling are separate follow-up changes. Deadline and archival migration Later migration of legacy COS deadline and archival responsibilities.

Before merging the API PR, reviewers need to agree on three deliberate choices:

  1. Include activeRevisions and objectCounts alongside conditions; retain all phase/object detail on COS.
  2. Define Available as owned installation health, allowing Available=True while a new desired revision cannot be created; Progressing carries the desired rollout.
  3. Use the condition-based pending timer and sticky timeout, clearing the timeout when the deadline is removed, without adding persisted timer fields.

The proposal selects these choices so subsequent PRs have a concrete baseline. Revision history configuration, ClusterExtension migration, slice storage, assertion redesign, rollback/pause APIs, and controller implementation are outside this document's change.

docs.title: Scenarios for subsequent PRs
docs.text:
Scenario Expected observation First COD, child not yet Ready One active child; Available=False and Progressing=True. Same template reapplied or deadline/root metadata edited No new COS; conditions reflect current observations. Healthy A; B creation denied Available=True; Progressing=True with the creation error, then False/ProgressDeadlineExceeded if configured. B created but its final phase is blocked A and B are active; Available=Unknown; each completed B phase extends its deadline. B finishes; existing COS archival completes One Ready child; Available=True and Progressing=False/NewClusterObjectSetProgressed. A restored after B A new higher immutable revision; no reactivation of an archived COS. Completed child becomes unhealthy Available=False; Progressing stays False/NewClusterObjectSetProgressed. Timed-out pending creation; template edited Still timed out until creation succeeds or the deadline is removed. Matching incomplete child; timeout then later phase progress Resume Progressing=True if the new milestone is within the interval. Restart during a stalled rollout Existing creation, phase, and condition timestamps determine the remaining window.

Implementation and migration note

Initially, the existing COS controller continues archiving predecessors. Moving archival and adding revisionHistoryLimit are follow-up changes. ClusterExtension continues creating COSs directly until it is migrated to use COD.

docs.title: E2E Test Isolation: Per-Scenario Catalogs via Dynamic OCI Image Building
Problem
docs.text: E2E test scenarios previously shared cluster-scoped resources (ClusterCatalogs, CRDs, packages), causing cascading failures when one scenario left state behind. Parallelism was impossible because scenarios conflicted on shared resource names.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Each scenario dynamically builds and pushes its own bundle and catalog OCI images at test time, parameterized by scenario ID. All cluster-scoped resource names include the scenario ID, making conflicts structurally impossible.

Scenario starts
  -> Generate parameterized bundle manifests (CRD names, deployments, etc. include scenario ID)
  -> Build + push bundle OCI images to e2e registry via go-containerregistry
  -> Generate FBC catalog config referencing those bundle image refs
  -> Build + push catalog OCI image to e2e registry
  -> Create ClusterCatalog pointing at the catalog image
  -> Run scenario steps
  -> Cleanup all resources (including catalog)

docs.title: Key Properties
docs.text:
• Every cluster-scoped resource name includes the scenario ID -- no conflicts by construction.
  • Failed scenario state is preserved for debugging without affecting other scenarios.
  • Parallelism (Concurrency > 1) is safe without further changes.
  • Adding new scenarios requires zero coordination with existing ones.

docs.title: Builder API (test/internal/catalog/)
docs.text:
Bundles are defined as components of a catalog. A single Build() call builds and pushes all bundle images, generates the FBC, and pushes the catalog image:

cat := catalog.NewCatalog("test", scenarioID,
    catalog.WithPackage("test",
        catalog.Bundle("1.0.0", catalog.WithCRD(), catalog.WithDeployment(), catalog.WithConfigMap()),
        catalog.Bundle("1.2.0", catalog.WithCRD(), catalog.WithDeployment()),
        catalog.Channel("beta", catalog.Entry("1.0.0"), catalog.Entry("1.2.0")),
    ),
)
result, err := cat.Build(ctx, "v1", localRegistry, clusterRegistry)
// result.CatalogName     = "test-catalog-{scenarioID}"
// result.CatalogImageRef = "{clusterRegistry}/e2e/test-catalog-{scenarioID}:v1"
// result.PackageNames    = {"test": "test-{scenarioID}"}

docs.title: Bundle Options
docs.text:
• WithCRD() -- CRD with group e2e-{id}.e2e.operatorframework.io
  • WithDeployment() -- Deployment named test-operator-{id} (includes CSV, script ConfigMap, NetworkPolicy)
  • WithConfigMap() -- additional test ConfigMap
  • WithInstallMode(modes...) -- sets supported install modes on the CSV
  • WithLargeCRD(fieldCount) -- CRD with many fields for large bundle testing
  • WithClusterRegistry(host) -- overrides the cluster-side registry host (for mirror testing)
  • StaticBundleDir(dir) -- reads pre-built bundle manifests without parameterization (e.g. webhook-operator)
  • BadImage() -- uses an invalid container image to trigger ImagePullBackOff
  • WithBundleProperty(type, value) -- adds a property to bundle metadata

docs.title: Feature File Conventions
docs.text:
Feature files define catalogs inline via data tables:

Background:
  Given OLM is available
  And an image registry is available
  And a catalog "test" with packages:
    | package | version | channel | replaces | contents                   |
    | test    | 1.0.0   | alpha   |          | CRD, Deployment, ConfigMap |
    | test    | 1.0.1   | alpha   | 1.0.0    | CRD, Deployment, ConfigMap |
    | test    | 1.2.0   | beta    |          | CRD, Deployment            |

docs.title: Variable Substitution
docs.text:
Templates in feature file YAML use these variables:

Variable Expansion Example ${NAME} ClusterExtension name ce-abc123 ${TEST_NAMESPACE} Scenario namespace ns-abc123 ${SCENARIO_ID} Unique scenario identifier abc123 ${PACKAGE:<name>} Parameterized package name test-abc123 ${CATALOG:<name>} ClusterCatalog resource name test-catalog-abc123 ${COS_NAME} ClusterObjectSet name cos-abc123

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text: Resource Pattern CRD group e2e-{id}.e2e.operatorframework.io Deployment test-operator-{id} Package name (FBC) {package}-{id} Bundle image {registry}/bundles/{package}-{id}:v{version} Catalog image {registry}/e2e/{name}-catalog-{id}:{tag} ClusterCatalog {name}-catalog-{id} Namespace ns-{id} ClusterExtension ce-{id}

docs.title: Registry Access
docs.text:
An in-cluster OCI registry (test/internal/registry/) stores bundle and catalog images. The registry runs as a ClusterIP Service; there is no NodePort or kind extraPortMappings.

The test runner reaches the registry via Kubernetes port-forward (SPDY through the API server), which works regardless of the cluster's network topology. A sync.OnceValues in the step definitions starts the port-forward once and returns the dynamically assigned localhost:<port> address used for all crane.Push / crane.Tag calls.

In-cluster components (e.g. the catalog unpacker) pull images using the Service DNS name (docker-registry.operator-controller-e2e.svc.cluster.local:5000), resolved by CoreDNS. Containerd on the node is never involved because the registry only holds OCI artifacts consumed by Go code, not container images for pods.

docs.title: Catalogd web server
docs.text:
Catalogd, the OLM v1 component for making catalog contents available on cluster, includes a web server that serves catalog contents to clients via HTTP(S) endpoints.

The endpoints to retrieve information about installable clusterextentions can be composed from the .status.urls.base of a ClusterCatalog resource with the selected access API path.

Currently, there are two API endpoints:

  1. api/v1/all endpoint that provides access to the FBC metadata in entirety.

As an example, to access the full FBC via the v1 API endpoint (indicated by path api/v1/all) where .status.urls.base is

    urls:
        base: https://catalogd-service.olmv1-system.svc/catalogs/operatorhubio

the URL to access the service would be https://catalogd-service.olmv1-system.svc/catalogs/operatorhubio/api/v1/all

  1. api/v1/metas endpoint that allows clients to retrieve filtered portions of the FBC.

The metas endpoint accepts parameters which are one of the sub-types of the Meta definition, following the pattern /api/v1/metas?<parameter>[&<parameter>...].

As an example, to access only the package schema blobs of the FBC via the api/v1/metas endpoint where .status.urls.base is

    urls:
        base: https://catalogd-service.olmv1-system.svc/catalogs/operatorhubio

the URL to access the service would be https://catalogd-service.olmv1-system.svc/catalogs/operatorhubio/api/v1/metas?schema=olm.package

For more examples of valid queries that can be made to the api/v1/metas service endpoint, please see Catalog Queries.

Note

The values of the .status.urls field in a ClusterCatalog resource are arbitrary string values and can change at any time. While there are no guarantees on the exact value of this field, it will always contain catalog-specific API endpoints for use by clients to make a request from within the cluster.

docs.title: Supported HTTP Methods
docs.text:
The HTTP request methods supported by the catalogd web server are:

  • GET
  • HEAD

docs.title: Response Format
docs.text:
Responses are encoded as a JSON Lines stream of File-Based Catalog (FBC) Meta objects delimited by newlines.

Example JSON-encoded FBC snippet 
{
    "schema": "olm.package",
    "name": "cockroachdb",
    "defaultChannel": "stable-v6.x",
}
{
    "schema": "olm.channel",
    "name": "stable-v6.x",
    "package": "cockroachdb",
    "entries": [
        {
            "name": "cockroachdb.v6.0.0",
            "skipRange": "<6.0.0"
        }
    ]
}
{
    "schema": "olm.bundle",
    "name": "cockroachdb.v6.0.0",
    "package": "cockroachdb",
    "image": "quay.io/openshift-community-operators/cockroachdb@sha256:d3016b1507515fc7712f9c47fd9082baf9ccb070aaab58ed0ef6e5abdedde8ba",
    "properties": [
        {
            "type": "olm.package",
            "value": {
                "packageName": "cockroachdb",
                "version": "6.0.0"
            }
        },
    ],
}

Corresponding JSON lines response: 

{"schema":"olm.package","name":"cockroachdb","defaultChannel":"stable-v6.x"}
{"schema":"olm.channel","name":"stable-v6.x","package":"cockroachdb","entries":[{"name":"cockroachdb.v6.0.0","skipRange":"<6.0.0"}]}
{"schema":"olm.bundle","name":"cockroachdb.v6.0.0","package":"cockroachdb","image":"quay.io/openshift-community-operators/cockroachdb@sha256:d3016b1507515fc7712f9c47fd9082baf9ccb070aaab58ed0ef6e5abdedde8ba","properties":[{"type":"olm.package","value":{"packageName":"cockroachdb","version":"6.0.0"}}]}

docs.title: Compression Support
docs.text:
The catalogd web server supports gzip compression of responses, which can significantly reduce associated network traffic. In order to signal that the client handles compressed responses, the client must include Accept-Encoding: gzip as a header in the HTTP request.

The web server will include a Content-Encoding: gzip header in compressed responses.

Note

Only catalogs whose uncompressed response body would result in a response size greater than 1400 bytes will be compressed.

docs.title: Cache Header Support
docs.text: For clients interested in caching the information returned from the catalogd web server, the Last-Modified header is set on responses and the If-Modified-Since header is supported for requests.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
OLMv1 uses Kubernetes NetworkPolicy to secure communication between components, restricting network traffic to only what's necessary for proper functionality.

  • The catalogd NetworkPolicy is implemented here.
  • The operator-controller is implemented here.

This document explains the details of NetworkPolicy implementation for the core components.

docs.title: Implementation Overview
docs.text:
NetworkPolicy is implemented for both catalogd and operator-controller components to:

  • Restrict incoming (ingress) traffic to only required ports and services
  • Control outgoing (egress) traffic patterns

Each component has a dedicated NetworkPolicy that applies to its respective pod through label selectors:

  • For catalogd: app.kubernetes.io/name=catalogd
  • For operator-controller: app.kubernetes.io/name=operator-controller

docs.title: Catalogd NetworkPolicy
docs.text:
• Ingress Rules Catalogd exposes three services, and its NetworkPolicy allows ingress traffic to the following TCP ports:

  • 7443: Metrics server for Prometheus metrics

  • 8443: Catalogd HTTPS server for catalog metadata API
  • 9443: Webhook server for Mutating Admission Webhook implementation

All other ingress traffic to the catalogd pod is blocked.

  • Egress Rules Catalogd needs to communicate with:

  • The Kubernetes API server

  • Image registries specified in ClusterCatalog objects

Currently, all egress traffic from catalogd is allowed, to support communication with arbitrary image registries that aren't known at install time.

docs.title: Operator-Controller NetworkPolicy
docs.text:
• Ingress Rules Operator-controller exposes one service, and its NetworkPolicy allows ingress traffic to:

  • 8443: Metrics server for Prometheus metrics

All other ingress traffic to the operator-controller pod is blocked.

  • Egress Rules Operator-controller needs to communicate with:

  • The Kubernetes API server

  • Catalogd's HTTPS server (on port 8443)
  • Image registries specified in bundle metadata

Currently, all egress traffic from operator-controller is allowed to support communication with arbitrary image registries that aren't known at install time.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
The current implementation focuses on securing ingress traffic while allowing all egress traffic. This approach:

  • Prevents unauthorized incoming connections
  • Allows communication with arbitrary image registries
  • Establishes a foundation for future refinements to egress rules

While allowing all egress does present some security risks, this implementation provides significant security improvements over having no network policies at all.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Network Issues
docs.text:
If you encounter network connectivity issues after deploying OLMv1, consider the following:

  • Verify NetworkPolicy support: Ensure your cluster has a CNI plugin that supports NetworkPolicy. If your Kubernetes cluster is using a Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin that doesn't support NetworkPolicy, then the NetworkPolicy resources you create will be completely ignored and have no effect whatsoever on traffic flow.
  • Check pod labels: Confirm that catalogd and operator-controller pods have the correct labels for NetworkPolicy selection:

# Verify catalogd pod labels
kubectl get pods -n olmv1-system --selector=apps.kubernetes.io/name=catalogd

# Verify operator-controller pod labels
kubectl get pods -n olmv1-system --selector=apps.kubernetes.io/name=operator-controller

# Compare with actual pod names
kubectl get pods -n olmv1-system | grep -E 'catalogd|operator-controller'
* Inspect logs: Check component logs for connection errors

For more comprehensive information on NetworkPolicy, see:

  • How NetworkPolicy is implemented with network plugins via the Container Network Interface (CNI)
  • Installing Network Policy Providers documentation.

docs.title: ClusterObjectSets
docs.text: This document explains what ClusterObjectSets are, how they enable safe phased rollouts of Kubernetes resources, and how operator-controller uses them to manage ClusterExtensions.

docs.title: What is a ClusterObjectSet?
docs.text:
A ClusterObjectSet is a cluster-scoped Kubernetes API that represents a versioned set of Kubernetes resources organized into ordered phases. It provides a declarative way to roll out a group of related resources sequentially, with built-in readiness checks between phases.

The revision content — the group identifier, revision number, collisionProtection strategy, and phases (including all objects within them) — is immutable once set. This guarantees that the record of what was deployed at a given revision cannot change after creation. Other fields like lifecycleState can change over the object's lifecycle (e.g. transitioning from Active to Archived), and optional fields like progressionProbes can be configured independently.

Each ClusterObjectSet has:

  • A group — a required, immutable identifier linking revisions into one sequence, regardless of their owner references
  • A revision number — an immutable, sequential integer that identifies the version
  • A lifecycle state — either Active (being reconciled) or Archived (inactive); transitions from Active to Archived but not back
  • A list of phases — immutable, ordered groups of Kubernetes objects that are applied sequentially
  • A collision protection strategy — immutable, controlling how pre-existing objects are handled
  • Status conditions — reporting rollout progress, availability, and success

ClusterObjectSets can be used by any controller or system that needs to manage the rollout of a set of Kubernetes resources in a controlled, phased manner. Within OLM, when BoxcutterRuntime is enabled, operator-controller creates and updates a ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) for each ClusterExtension. The COD controller creates the immutable ClusterObjectSet revisions that deploy and upgrade the extension.

For a standalone walkthrough that manages mutable desired content through COS revisions, see Manage standalone ClusterObjectDeployments.

The group value must be 1–52 characters long, start with a lowercase letter, contain only lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, and end with a letter or digit. Set metadata.name explicitly to <group>-<revision>, with the revision in decimal and without leading zeros. Revisions range from 1 to 9999999999, inclusive: ten digits plus the separating hyphen fit within a 63-character name even for a 52-character group. This naming rule ensures that a group cannot contain duplicate revision numbers. Name generation through metadata.generateName is not supported.

Revisions in the same group can transfer managed objects between them even when they have different controller owners or no owner references. They share the server-side apply field manager cos-group/<group>. Different groups remain subject to normal object collision protection.

docs.title: Revision membership and management
docs.text:
The immutable spec.group identifies a COS's revision chain. Controller owner references record management relationships: a COD owns the COS revisions it creates, and each COS owns the Kubernetes objects it manages.

A standalone COS, a COD-owned COS, and a COS owned by another controller are siblings when their groups match. Adding, changing, or removing a COS's controller owner reference leaves its revision chain unchanged. For example, deleting a COD with orphan propagation removes its owner references from the surviving COSs; those COSs remain in the same group and retain the same handoff behavior. Archived and deleting COSs are excluded from the active sibling list.

docs.title: Controller deployment
docs.text:
The experimental object-controller runs in its own Deployment with its own service account and leader-election lease. It watches ClusterObjectDeployments, ClusterObjectSets, and the objects they manage; it does not require ClusterExtension or ClusterCatalog resources or controllers. When BoxcutterRuntime is enabled, operator-controller resolves and unpacks bundles, applies ClusterObjectDeployments, and observes their rollout status.

The Helm chart automatically enables object-controller alongside operator-controller when BoxcutterRuntime is enabled. To deploy it independently, first build an image and make it available to your cluster (push it to a registry, or load it into your local cluster). Set the image reference below, then render and apply the manifests:

helm template object-controller helm/olmv1 \
  --set options.featureSet=experimental \
  --set options.objectController.enabled=true \
  --set options.operatorController.enabled=false \
  --set options.catalogd.enabled=false \
  --set-string options.objectController.deployment.image='<your-built-image>' \
  > object-controller.yaml
kubectl apply -f object-controller.yaml
kubectl -n olmv1-system rollout status deployment/object-controller-controller-manager --timeout=180s

Set options.objectController.deployment.image to the built image when using a local or downstream image. make go-build-local builds bin/object-controller; make docker-build builds its image alongside the existing controller images. OBJECT_CONTROLLER_IMAGE_REPO controls its build and release repository.

Object-controller reads immutable referenced Secrets directly from the API server in the namespace specified by each reference. Metrics require a TLS certificate and key; the chart configures these through cert-manager or the OpenShift service CA when enabled. The minimal standalone example above enables neither certificate provider, so metrics are disabled. Health and readiness probes remain enabled. The default service account has cluster-admin privileges because ClusterObjectSets can manage arbitrary Kubernetes resources, matching the existing experimental runtime.

For downstream builds enabling BoxcutterRuntime, package the new binary and configure its image in addition to the operator-controller image. It is possible to package both binaries in one image while running them in separate Deployments. Standard installations and default Helm installations without BoxcutterRuntime do not enable object-controller.

docs.title: Why ClusterObjectSets?
docs.text:
ClusterObjectSets solve several problems that arise when managing sets of related Kubernetes resources:

  • Immutable revision content — The revision number, phases, objects, and collision protection strategy are immutable once set, providing a clear, auditable record of exactly what was deployed at each revision. There is no ambiguity about what resources belong to a given version.
  • Phased rollout — Resources are grouped into phases (e.g. CRDs before Deployments) and applied sequentially. A phase only progresses after all its objects pass readiness probes, preventing partially-applied states.
  • Safe transitions — During a revision change, both the old and new revisions remain active until the new revision fully rolls out. Object ownership transitions from one revision to the next, ensuring no resource is left unmanaged.
  • Single ownership — Each Kubernetes resource can only be managed by one ClusterObjectSet at a time. This prevents conflicts between revisions fighting over the same object.
  • Large resource support — Object manifests can be stored inline or externalized into Secrets via references, allowing ClusterObjectSets to manage bundles that would otherwise exceed etcd's 1.5 MiB object size limit.

docs.title: Active state
docs.text:
When a ClusterObjectSet is Active, the controller actively reconciles it using the boxcutter library:

  • Phases are applied sequentially, each waiting for readiness before proceeding
  • Objects are managed via server-side apply
  • Status conditions are updated to reflect rollout progress

docs.title: Revision transitions
docs.text:
When transitioning from one revision to the next:

  1. A new ClusterObjectSet is created with the same group and the next sequential revision number
  2. Both old and new revisions remain Active during the transition
  3. Objects transition ownership from the old revision to the new one
  4. Once the new revision has rolled out successfully, the old revision can be archived

docs.title: Archival
docs.text:
When a revision's lifecycle state is set to Archived:

  • It is removed from the owner list of all previously managed objects
  • Objects that did not transition to a succeeding revision are deleted
  • The revision cannot be un-archived
  • It remains in the cluster for historical reference until garbage collected

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
Objects within a ClusterObjectSet are organized into phases. Each phase groups related resources, and phases are applied sequentially. Within a phase, all objects are applied simultaneously in no particular order.

A phase only progresses to the next after all of its objects pass their readiness probes. This ensures dependencies are satisfied before dependents are created — for example, CRDs are established before Deployments that use custom resources.

Phase names follow the DNS label standard (RFC 1123) and must be unique within a ClusterObjectSet. A ClusterObjectSet supports up to 20 phases, with up to 50 objects per phase.

docs.title: Phase ordering in operator-controller
docs.text:
When operator-controller creates a ClusterObjectSet for a ClusterExtension, it automatically assigns objects to phases based on their GroupKind:

Order Phase Resource Kinds 1 namespaces Namespace 2 policies NetworkPolicy, PodDisruptionBudget, PriorityClass 3 identity ServiceAccount 4 configuration Secret, ConfigMap 5 storage PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim, StorageClass 6 crds CustomResourceDefinition 7 roles ClusterRole, Role 8 bindings ClusterRoleBinding, RoleBinding 9 infrastructure Service, Issuer (cert-manager) 10 deploy Certificate (cert-manager), Deployment 11 scaling VerticalPodAutoscaler 12 publish PrometheusRule, ServiceMonitor, PodMonitor, Ingress, Route, ConsoleYAMLSample, ConsoleQuickStart, ConsoleCLIDownload, ConsoleLink, ConsolePlugin 13 admission ValidatingWebhookConfiguration, MutatingWebhookConfiguration

Any resource kind not listed above defaults to the deploy phase.

Note

This phase ordering is specific to how operator-controller creates ClusterObjectSets. The API itself does not enforce any particular phase ordering — phases are applied in the order they appear in the spec.phases list.

docs.title: Readiness probes
docs.text:
A phase only progresses to the next after all of its objects pass readiness probes. Several resource kinds have built-in probes:

Resource Kind Readiness Criteria CustomResourceDefinition Condition Established = True Namespace status.phase = "Active" PersistentVolumeClaim status.phase = "Bound" Deployment status.updatedReplicas == status.replicas and condition Available = True StatefulSet status.updatedReplicas == status.replicas and condition Available = True Certificate (cert-manager) Condition Ready = True Issuer (cert-manager) Condition Ready = True

For custom resources or other objects that need tailored checks, you can define custom progression probes in the spec.progressionProbes field. These are experimental and support three assertion types:

ConditionEqual Checks that an object has a condition of the specified type and status (e.g. Ready = True). FieldsEqual Checks that the values at two field paths match (e.g. spec.replicas == status.readyReplicas). FieldValue Checks that a field has a specific value (e.g. status.phase = "Bound").

Probes use selectors to target objects by GroupKind or by label. A probe only runs against objects matching its selector — if no objects in a phase match, the probe is considered to have passed.

docs.title: Collision protection
docs.text:
Collision protection controls whether a ClusterObjectSet can adopt pre-existing objects on the cluster. This is configured at three levels, with the most specific taking precedence:

object > phase > spec

The available strategies are:

Prevent Only manages objects the revision created itself. This is the safest option and prevents ownership collisions entirely. IfNoController Can adopt pre-existing objects that are not owned by another controller. Useful when taking over management of manually-created resources. None Can adopt any pre-existing object, even if owned by another controller. Use with extreme caution — this can cause multiple controllers to fight over the same resource.

docs.title: Object storage: inline vs. references
docs.text:
Each object in a phase can be stored in one of two ways (exactly one must be set):

object The full Kubernetes manifest is embedded inline in the ClusterObjectSet. Simple and self-contained, but contributes to the overall size of the ClusterObjectSet resource in etcd. ref A reference to a Secret that holds the serialized object manifest. The ref specifies the Secret name, namespace, and data key containing either a JSON-encoded manifest or gzip-compressed JSON bytes. This allows ClusterObjectSets to manage bundles that would otherwise exceed etcd's 1.5 MiB object size limit.

When operator-controller renders ClusterObjectDeployment templates for ClusterExtensions, it automatically externalizes objects into immutable Secrets:

  • Secrets are packed up to 900 KiB each, leaving headroom below the etcd limit
  • Objects larger than 900 KiB are gzip-compressed before storage (ref resolution auto-detects and transparently decompresses gzip-compressed values so consumers see the original JSON manifest)
  • Content-addressable naming (based on SHA-256 hashes of the data) ensures that Secret names and data keys are deterministic, making creation idempotent and safe to retry

For a detailed design discussion, see Large Bundle Support.

docs.title: Status conditions
docs.text: ClusterObjectSets report a single Ready condition describing their current state. Rollout completion is recorded separately as a timestamp in status.completedAt, not as a condition.

docs.title: Ready
docs.text:
Indicates whether all objects in the revision have been successfully rolled out and reached their desired state.

Status Reason Meaning True AllObjectsReady All objects are at the desired state False ObjectsNotReady One or more objects are still being applied or have not yet passed their readiness probes during rollout False Superseded One or more objects have been adopted by a newer revision of the object set False ObjectCollision One or more objects are controlled by another owner, or are unowned and collision protection prevents adoption False PreconditionsNotMet A precondition for applying the revision is not yet satisfied (a referenced Secret is mutable or has invalid or changed content, or a preflight dry-run was rejected, e.g. an immutable field, a conflicting object, or RBAC/dependency CRDs not yet propagated); the revision keeps retrying and recovers once the precondition is met False InvalidSpecification The revision spec is invalid (a malformed revision/phase object or progression probe); requires a spec change False Archiving The revision is being archived; owned objects are still being torn down False Archived Objects torn down after archival Unknown Pending The revision has not yet been evaluated (initial state)

On a revision's first reconciliation the Ready condition is initialized to Unknown/Pending, so it is always present. A transient internal error (e.g. an API read failure) leaves the Ready condition unchanged and is retried with backoff; it is not reported as a distinct reason (while the revision is still Pending, it stays Unknown/Pending).

docs.title: Progress deadline
docs.text:
The progress deadline is a ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) concept: the time allowed for the deployment to progress to its desired new revision. Configure it through spec.template.spec.progressDeadlineMinutes. The COD enforces this budget itself; the ClusterObjectSets it creates do not carry a deadline. Time spent waiting for the ClusterObjectSet to be created is not counted, and each new revision receives its own budget, measured from the revision's creation timestamp until its first successful rollout (recorded in status.completedAt). Completing a phase does not reset the timer.

If the desired revision is still incomplete when that budget expires, the COD reports Progressing=False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded. A five-phase revision with a ten-minute deadline has ten minutes total, even if four phases have completed. The COD schedules a deadline check even if the COS emits no further events.

The COS's Ready condition continues to report readiness failures, such as ObjectsNotReady, PreconditionsNotMet, or InvalidSpecification. The COD checks elapsed time independently of the COS's readiness condition.

Omitting the field disables the deadline. Reconciliation continues after a timeout, so a revision can still complete later. Once status.completedAt is recorded, the COD reports Progressing=False with reason NewClusterObjectSetProgressed. Later health regressions do not restart deadline timing. The COD can remain Available=True if an older active revision is still ready.

docs.title: ClusterObjectDeployment Progressing
docs.text:
A ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) reports rollout progress and ownership conflicts on its Progressing condition. While a rollout is incomplete, it also reflects why its head active revision is not yet Ready, so you can tell a rollout that is merely in progress from one that is stalled on something you must fix. For revision failures, inspect the named ClusterObjectSet for the specific cause.

Status Reason Meaning What to do True NewClusterObjectSetProgressing The head revision is rolling out (Pending/ObjectsNotReady) Wait True RevisionPreconditionsNotMet The head revision's precondition is not yet met (e.g. a mutable/invalid referenced Secret, or RBAC/dependency CRDs not yet propagated); it keeps retrying Satisfy the precondition (grant RBAC, install the dependency, fix the Secret); it recovers automatically False RevisionObjectCollision The head revision's objects are owned by another controller or already exist; it will not roll out without intervention Resolve ownership of the conflicting objects False RevisionInvalidSpecification The head revision's own objects are invalid Correct the template so the rendered objects are valid False ProgressDeadlineExceeded A still-retrying revision exceeded its deadline (see Progress deadline) See above False InvalidSpecification The deployment's own spec.template.metadata is invalid, so no revision is created Fix the template labels/annotations False OwnerConflict The highest active, non-deleting revision in the deployment's group is controlled by another controller; no new revision is created Resolve the revision's controller ownership, or archive or delete the conflicting revision False NewClusterObjectSetProgressed The head revision completed its rollout None

OwnerConflict concerns ownership of the ClusterObjectSet itself, while RevisionObjectCollision concerns ownership of objects within a revision. OwnerConflict takes precedence even if an owned revision has completed or exceeded its progress deadline. Availability still depends only on owned active revisions; a previous ready revision can keep the COD Available=True during the conflict.

For a ClusterExtension, OwnerConflict maps to Progressing=True with reason Retrying, preserving the deployment's message about the conflicting revision and its controller. A first install reports Installed=False with reason Failed. During an upgrade, the previously installed bundle and its Installed=True condition are preserved until the new rollout completes, with observedGeneration updated to acknowledge the current spec. Reconciliation resumes automatically when the ownership conflict clears.

RevisionObjectCollision and RevisionInvalidSpecification are hard stalls: they will not resolve on their own, so they report Progressing=False and take precedence over ProgressDeadlineExceeded (the actionable cause is more useful than "the clock ran out"). RevisionPreconditionsNotMet keeps retrying, so it stays Progressing=True and the progress deadline still governs it. Note that RevisionInvalidSpecification (the revision's rendered objects) is distinct from the deployment's own InvalidSpecification (invalid spec.template.metadata, reported before any revision is created).

docs.title: Completion (status.completedAt)
docs.text: The first time a revision becomes ready, the controller stamps status.completedAt with the current time. This timestamp is set once and never changes, marking that this revision successfully rolled out at least once — it persists even if the revision later becomes not ready. The ClusterExtension controller uses it to determine the installed revision.

docs.title: How operator-controller uses ClusterObjectSets
docs.text: With BoxcutterRuntime enabled, ClusterObjectSets serve as the deployment mechanism for ClusterExtensions. The operator-controller is one consumer of the ClusterObjectSet API.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
When a ClusterExtension is installed:

  1. The operator-controller resolves a bundle from the catalog
  2. The bundle's Kubernetes manifests are sorted into phases by resource kind
  3. Objects are packed into immutable Secrets
  4. The operator-controller applies a ClusterObjectDeployment with the desired content in its template
  5. When a new revision is needed, the COD controller creates an Active ClusterObjectSet with a revision number one greater than the highest existing revision in the group (1 for an empty group)
  6. Phases roll out sequentially — each phase waits for all its objects to become ready before the next phase begins

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
When a ClusterExtension is upgraded to a new version:

  1. The operator-controller updates the ClusterObjectDeployment's template with the new bundle content
  2. The COD controller creates a new ClusterObjectSet with a revision number one greater than the highest existing revision in the group, including archived and foreign-owned ClusterObjectSets
  3. Both old and new revisions are Active during the transition
  4. Objects transition ownership from the old revision to the new one
  5. Once the new revision has rolled out successfully, the old revision is archived
  6. The COD controller garbage collects older archived revisions, keeping the last 5 by default for auditing

Once a group reaches revision 9999999999, the ClusterObjectDeployment controller reports an error instead of allocating another revision. Reconciliation of unchanged content still works when no higher active, non-deleting COS is controlled by another controller.

docs.title: Relationship with ClusterExtension
docs.text:
A ClusterExtension owns a ClusterObjectDeployment with the same name. The COD owns the ClusterObjectSet revisions it creates, and each COS owns its managed Kubernetes objects. These controller owner references enable cascading garbage collection when the extension is deleted.

The COD controller sets each revision's spec.group to the COD's name, which is also the ClusterExtension's name. Revision lookup uses the group; labels and owner references do not determine membership.

The COD template propagates labels that identify the parent extension to its COS revisions:

metadata:
  labels:
    olm.operatorframework.io/owner-kind: ClusterExtension
    olm.operatorframework.io/owner-name: my-extension

docs.title: Inline objects
docs.text:
This example shows a ClusterObjectSet with objects embedded directly in the spec. This is the simplest approach and works well when the total size of all objects stays within etcd's 1.5 MiB limit.

apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterObjectSet
metadata:
  name: my-app-1
spec:
  group: my-app
  revision: 1
  lifecycleState: Active
  collisionProtection: Prevent
  phases:
  - name: crds
    objects:
    - object:
        apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
        kind: CustomResourceDefinition
        metadata:
          name: widgets.example.com
        spec:
          group: example.com
          names:
            kind: Widget
            plural: widgets
          scope: Namespaced
          versions:
          - name: v1
            served: true
            storage: true
            schema:
              openAPIV3Schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  spec:
                    type: object
  - name: rbac
    objects:
    - object:
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: ServiceAccount
        metadata:
          name: my-app-controller
          namespace: my-app-system
    - object:
        apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
        kind: ClusterRole
        metadata:
          name: my-app-manager-role
        rules:
        - apiGroups: ["example.com"]
          resources: ["widgets"]
          verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "delete"]
  - name: deploy
    objects:
    - object:
        apiVersion: apps/v1
        kind: Deployment
        metadata:
          name: my-app-controller
          namespace: my-app-system
        spec:
          replicas: 1
          selector:
            matchLabels:
              app: my-app-controller
          template:
            metadata:
              labels:
                app: my-app-controller
            spec:
              serviceAccountName: my-app-controller
              containers:
              - name: manager
                image: example.com/my-app-controller:v1.0.0

docs.title: Secret references
docs.text:
This example shows a ClusterObjectSet that references objects stored in Secrets. This is how operator-controller creates ClusterObjectSets, and is necessary when managing bundles with large resources like CRDs with extensive schemas.

Object manifests are stored in immutable Secrets. Secret names are content-addressable, computed as <revisionName>-<16 hex chars> where the suffix is the first 8 bytes of a SHA-256 digest over the Secret's sorted keys and values. Each data key is a 43-character base64url-encoded (no padding) SHA-256 hash of the stored object bytes.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: my-app-1-3a7f1b9c0e2d4f68
  namespace: olmv1-system
immutable: true
data:
  # key: 43-char base64url SHA-256 of the object JSON bytes
  # value: base64-encoded JSON-serialized Kubernetes manifest
  K8sTl2xQa0vNpR7mW4dYcJfHbE9gUiAoZX1sDj6wFCy: <base64-encoded CRD JSON>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: my-app-1-8b2e4a6c1d3f5097
  namespace: olmv1-system
immutable: true
data:
  # Multiple objects can be packed into the same Secret
  Pm5tRqLwXv8sCj3kFdNhYe7bUiA0oZG1x2W9acDfHJy: <base64-encoded ServiceAccount JSON>
  Vn4mTsLwXp8rCk3jFdNhYe7bUiA0oZG1x2W9acDfHQy: <base64-encoded ClusterRole JSON>
  Bq9nRtLxYw2sDk4lGePhZf8cVjB1pUiA0oZH3x5WaCdy: <base64-encoded Deployment JSON>

The ClusterObjectSet references these Secrets:

apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterObjectSet
metadata:
  name: my-app-1
spec:
  group: my-app
  revision: 1
  lifecycleState: Active
  collisionProtection: Prevent
  phases:
  - name: crds
    objects:
    - ref:
        name: my-app-1-3a7f1b9c0e2d4f68
        namespace: olmv1-system
        key: "K8sTl2xQa0vNpR7mW4dYcJfHbE9gUiAoZX1sDj6wFCy"
  - name: rbac
    objects:
    - ref:
        name: my-app-1-8b2e4a6c1d3f5097
        namespace: olmv1-system
        key: "Pm5tRqLwXv8sCj3kFdNhYe7bUiA0oZG1x2W9acDfHJy"
    - ref:
        name: my-app-1-8b2e4a6c1d3f5097
        namespace: olmv1-system
        key: "Vn4mTsLwXp8rCk3jFdNhYe7bUiA0oZG1x2W9acDfHQy"
  - name: deploy
    objects:
    - ref:
        name: my-app-1-8b2e4a6c1d3f5097
        namespace: olmv1-system
        key: "Bq9nRtLxYw2sDk4lGePhZf8cVjB1pUiA0oZH3x5WaCdy"

Multiple objects can reference different keys within the same Secret, allowing efficient packing of smaller objects.

docs.title: Inspecting ClusterObjectSets
docs.text:
# List all ClusterObjectSets
kubectl get clusterobjectsets

# List revisions in a specific extension's group
kubectl get clusterobjectsets --field-selector spec.group=my-extension

# View full details for a specific revision
kubectl get clusterobjectset <name> -o yaml

# Inspect reconciliation in the independent controller
kubectl -n olmv1-system logs deployment/object-controller-controller-manager

Example output:

NAME                   GROUP          READY     AGE
my-extension-1         my-extension   Unknown   2d
my-extension-2         my-extension   True      1h

docs.title: Need
docs.text:
ClusterObjectSet (COS) objects embed full Kubernetes manifests inline in .spec.phases[].objects[].object. With up to 20 phases and 50 objects per phase, the serialized COS can approach or exceed the etcd maximum object size of 1.5 MiB. Large operators shipping many CRDs, Deployments, RBAC rules, and webhook configurations are likely to hit this limit.

When the limit is exceeded, the API server rejects the COS and the extension cannot be installed or upgraded. Today there is no mitigation path other than reducing the number of objects in the bundle.

The phases data is immutable after creation, write-once/read-many, and only consumed by the revision reconciler — making it a good candidate for externalization.

This document presents two approaches for solving this problem. Per-object content references is the preferred approach; externalized phases to Secret chains is presented as an alternative.

docs.title: Approach: Per-Object Content References
docs.text: Externalize all objects by default. Add an optional ref field to ClusterObjectSetObject that points to the object content stored in a Secret. Exactly one of object or ref must be set. The system uses ref for all objects it creates; users who manually craft COSs may use either object or ref.

docs.title: API change
docs.text:
Add a new ObjectSourceRef type and a ref field to ClusterObjectSetObject. Exactly one of object or ref must be set, enforced via CEL validation. Both fields are immutable (inherited from the immutability of phases).

type ClusterObjectSetObject struct {
    // object is an optional embedded Kubernetes object to be applied.
    // Exactly one of object or ref must be set.
    //
    // +kubebuilder:validation:EmbeddedResource
    // +kubebuilder:pruning:PreserveUnknownFields
    // +optional
    Object *unstructured.Unstructured `json:"object,omitempty"`

    // ref is an optional reference to a Secret that holds the serialized
    // object manifest.
    // Exactly one of object or ref must be set.
    //
    // +optional
    Ref *ObjectSourceRef `json:"ref,omitempty"`

    // collisionProtection controls whether the operator can adopt and modify
    // objects that already exist on the cluster.
    //
    // +optional
    // +kubebuilder:validation:Enum=Prevent;IfNoController;None
    CollisionProtection CollisionProtection `json:"collisionProtection,omitempty"`
}

CEL validation on ClusterObjectSetObject:

rule: "has(self.object) != has(self.ref)"
message: "exactly one of object or ref must be set"

docs.title: ObjectSourceRef
docs.text:
// ObjectSourceRef references content within a Secret that contains a
// serialized object manifest.
type ObjectSourceRef struct {
    // name is the name of the referenced Secret.
    //
    // +required
    // +kubebuilder:validation:MinLength=1
    // +kubebuilder:validation:MaxLength=253
    Name string `json:"name"`

    // namespace is the namespace of the referenced Secret.
    //
    // +optional
    // +kubebuilder:validation:MaxLength=63
    Namespace string `json:"namespace,omitempty"`

    // key is the data key within the referenced Secret containing the
    // object manifest content. The value at this key must be a
    // JSON-serialized Kubernetes object manifest.
    //
    // +required
    // +kubebuilder:validation:MinLength=1
    // +kubebuilder:validation:MaxLength=253
    Key string `json:"key"`
}

docs.title: Content format
docs.text:
The content at the referenced key is a JSON-serialized Kubernetes manifest — the same structure currently used inline in the object field.

Content may optionally be gzip-compressed. The reconciler auto-detects compression by inspecting the first two bytes of the content: gzip streams always start with the magic bytes \x1f\x8b. If detected, the content is decompressed before JSON deserialization. Otherwise, the content is treated as plain JSON. This makes compression transparent — no additional API fields or annotations are needed, and producers can choose per-key whether to compress.

Kubernetes manifests are highly repetitive structured text and typically achieve 5-10x size reduction with gzip, following the same pattern used by Helm for release storage.

To inspect an uncompressed referenced object stored in a Secret:

kubectl get secret <name> -o jsonpath='{.data.<key>}' | base64 -d | jq .

To inspect a gzip-compressed referenced object stored in a Secret:

kubectl get secret <name> -o jsonpath='{.data.<key>}' | base64 -d | gunzip | jq .

docs.title: Referenced resource conventions
docs.text:
The COS API does not enforce any particular structure or metadata on the referenced Secret — the ref field is a plain pointer. The reconciler only requires that the Secret exists and that the key resolves to valid JSON content (optionally gzip-compressed). Everything else is a convention that the system follows when it creates referenced Secrets, and that other producers should follow for consistency and safe lifecycle management.

Recommended conventions:

  1. Secret type: Secrets should use the dedicated type olm.operatorframework.io/object-data to distinguish them from user-created Secrets and enable easy identification. The system always sets this type on Secrets it creates. The reconciler does not enforce the Secret type when resolving refs, but it does enforce that referenced Secrets have immutable: true set and that their content has not changed since first resolution.

  2. Immutability: Secrets must set immutable: true. The reconciler verifies that all referenced Secrets have immutable: true set before proceeding. Mutable referenced Secrets are rejected and the ClusterObjectSet reports Ready=False, Reason=PreconditionsNotMet. Additionally, the reconciler records content hashes of the resolved phases on first successful reconciliation and reports the same condition if the content changes (e.g., if a Secret is deleted and recreated with the same name but different data).

  3. Owner references: Referenced Secrets should carry an ownerReference to the COS so that Kubernetes garbage collection removes them when the COS is deleted: 

    ownerReferences:
  - apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
    kind: ClusterObjectSet
    name: <COS-name>
    uid: <revision-uid>
    controller: true
    Without an ownerReference, the producer is responsible for cleaning up the Secret when the COS is deleted. The reconciler does not delete referenced Secrets itself.

  4. Revision label: A label identifying the owning revision aids discovery, debugging, and bulk cleanup: 

    olm.operatorframework.io/revision-name: <COS-name>
    This enables fetching all referenced Secrets for a revision with a single list call: 
    kubectl get secrets -l olm.operatorframework.io/revision-name=my-extension-1

Multiple externalized objects may share a single Secret by using different keys. This reduces the number of Secrets created.

docs.title: Controller implementation
docs.text:
The ClusterExtension controller externalizes all objects by default. When the Boxcutter applier creates a COS, every object entry uses ref pointing to the object content stored in a Secret. Secrets are created in the system namespace (olmv1-system by default). This keeps COSs uniformly small regardless of bundle size.

Users who manually craft COSs may use either inline object or ref pointing to their own Secrets. Inline object is convenient for development, testing, or extensions with very few small objects. Users who prefer to manage their own externalized storage can create Secrets and use ref directly.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A system-created COS with all objects externalized:

apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterObjectSet
metadata:
  name: my-extension-1
spec:
  group: my-extension
  revision: 1
  lifecycleState: Active
  collisionProtection: Prevent
  phases:
    - name: rbac
      objects:
        - ref:
            name: my-extension-1-rbac
            namespace: olmv1-system
            key: service-account
        - ref:
            name: my-extension-1-rbac
            namespace: olmv1-system
            key: cluster-role
    - name: crds
      objects:
        - ref:
            name: my-extension-1-crds
            namespace: olmv1-system
            key: my-crd
    - name: deploy
      objects:
        - ref:
            name: my-extension-1-deploy
            namespace: olmv1-system
            key: deployment
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: my-extension-1-rbac
  namespace: olmv1-system
  labels:
    olm.operatorframework.io/revision-name: my-extension-1
  ownerReferences:
