ART (Doozer) syncs source → distgit → builds; a config that references a missing Dockerfile fails that image's build, and because it is a payload member it can degrade/block the nightly payload assembly and page ART / the component owners. → Phase 1 is a hard prerequisite for Phase 2. - A for_payload: true image that no operator references via image-references is flagged by the release controller as an unreferenced payload image. → for_payload: true must not be enabled until cluster-olm-operator's image-references entry (Phase 3a) is in place. - Therefore stage the ocp-build-data onboarding: (1) ART onboarding request (distgit/delivery creation) can start now, in parallel, with no code dependency; (2) add the image config only after the Dockerfile lands, and introduce it non-payload first (for_payload: false / disabled) to shake out the build without touching the payload; (3) flip for_payload: true only once the build is green and the consumer reference (Phase 3a) exists. The image build is onboarded on two independent tracks, both of which depend on the Phase 1 Dockerfile. Only the ART onboarding request (distgit creation) has no code dependency and should start immediately.

Track A — CI build (openshift/release). Lighter, self-serve; this is what makes the image available in CI and spliced into the e2e payload that cluster-olm-operator e2e boots from (gates Phase 3). - PR to openshift/release adding, under images.items in each ci-operator/config/openshift/operator-framework-operator-controller/openshift-...-<branch>.yaml: { dockerfile_path: openshift/object-controller.Dockerfile, to: olm-object-controller } (plus the from:/inputs:/build_args: form in the __okd-scos variants). Run make update / make jobs to regenerate. - No promotion change needed: the existing block auto-promotes olm-object-controller to ocp/<ver>, and releases.latest.integration.include_built_images: true splices it into the e2e payload. Consumed via the payload, not via explicit dependencies:. - Approvals: DPTP + repo OWNERS.

Track B — ART production onboarding (ocp-build-data + ART). Heavyweight, long lead. - Start now (no code dependency): file the ART onboarding request; ART creates distgit ose-olm-object-controller-container (rhaos-{MAJOR}.{MINOR}-rhel-9) and delivery repo openshift4/ose-olm-object-controller-rhel9. - ocp-build-data images/ose-olm-object-controller.yml (produced in Phase 2), payload_name: olm-object-controller, introduced non-payload/disabled first. - CVP / release-payload acceptance for the new payload member. - for_payload: true flipped last (Phase 2 step 3), coupled to the Phase 3a image-references entry. - Confirm the component appears in the CI release payload consumed by cluster-olm-operator e2e before the Phase 3b crossover.

Naming: use olm-object-controller consistently — CI to: name, ocp-build-data payload_name, and the cluster-olm-operator image-references entry — matching olm-operator-controller / olm-catalogd.

  • CI impact: none on existing repos until the image is referenced.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Downstream fork: add object-controller build assets (additive)
docs.text:
Repo: openshift/operator-framework-operator-controller. - Add openshift/object-controller.Dockerfile mirroring catalogd.Dockerfile: runtime stage copies only /object-controller, plus openshift/object-controller/cp-manifests, helm/olmv1, openshift/helm/experimental.yaml, and openshift/helm/object-controller.yaml→openshift.yaml. - Add openshift/object-controller/cp-manifests (DEST ${1}/helm/object-controller). - Add openshift/helm/object-controller.yaml: - namespaces.olmv1.name: openshift-object-controller - options.objectController.enabled left unset (null) — see enablement resolution below. - options.objectController.deployment.image: ${OBJECT_CONTROLLER_IMAGE} and .replicas: 1 (the deployment template requires replicas). - options.operatorController.enabled: false, options.catalogd.enabled: false - options.openshift.enabled: true, featureSet: standard - deployments.templateSpec mirrors the siblings, anti-affinity keyed on control-plane: object-controller-controller-manager.

Enablement resolution (RESOLVED — was an open item). The helper (_helpers.tpl:82-83) fails a render when objectController.enabled is truthy but featureSet != experimental, and with operatorController.enabled: false the null-default can never turn it on. So object-controller.yaml must not hardcode enabled: true (that would crash the standard render that cluster-olm-operator does on non-TechPreview clusters). Instead it leaves enabled unset → the component renders empty and non-failing on standard (verified: only the namespace + default-deny NetworkPolicy), and cluster-olm-operator sets options.objectController.enabled=true for the object-controller render only when it is already rendering experimental + BoxcutterRuntime (Phase 3b). - Update openshift/helm/generate-manifests.sh to emit openshift/object-controller/manifests.yaml (shipped values → namespace-only) and manifests-experimental.yaml rendered with --values experimental.yaml --set options.objectController.enabled=true so the separated render is reviewable and the standalone render is verified in the snapshot. Commit the snapshots.

Verified (helm template): the forced-on experimental render produces the object-controller Deployment/Service/SA/ServiceMonitor/NetworkPolicy/RBAC and the clusterobjectsets CRD, all in openshift-object-controller, image ${OBJECT_CONTROLLER_IMAGE}, with zero operator-controller/catalogd leakage.

Heads-up (pre-existing, out of scope): regenerating the downstream snapshots shows the committed openshift/{catalogd,operator-controller}/manifests*.yaml on main are already stale vs the current chart (e.g. a missing operator-controller-manager-role ClusterRole). The Phase 1 PR must stay scoped to object-controller and not absorb that drift; it should be fixed in a separate regeneration PR. - Leave operator-controller.Dockerfile and operator-controller.yaml unchanged (object-controller binary still baked in; passenger block still present). Purely additive. - CI impact: fork CI builds an additional image / snapshot; nothing consumes it yet → green.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Build-config onboarding: CI + ART (additive)
docs.text:
Both artifacts depend on the Phase 1 Dockerfile.

2-CI — openshift/release (Track A). Add the olm-object-controller image stanza (see Phase 0 Track A) to every relevant operator-framework-operator-controller-<branch>.yaml (and __okd-scos variant). Merge → postsubmit builds and promotes it to ocp/<ver>; e2e payloads now include it. This is the gate for Phase 3 e2e consumption.

2-ART — openshift/ocp-build-data (Track B). Per target branch (openshift-4.21, and openshift-4.20 if backporting), add images/ose-olm-object-controller.yml mirroring ose-olm-operator-controller.yml: content.source.dockerfile: openshift/object-controller.Dockerfile, same git source (the fork), payload_name: olm-object-controller, name: openshift4/ose-olm-object-controller-rhel9, matching distgit/delivery. - Introduce non-payload/disabled first (for_payload: false) to shake out the build without touching the nightly payload. - Flip for_payload: true only after the build is green and the cluster-olm-operator image-references entry exists (Phase 3a) — otherwise the release controller flags an unreferenced payload image. - CI impact: adds an image to the build; nothing references it yet; payload membership deferred to the coupled flip. Gated by Phase 0 ART onboarding.

docs.title: Phase 3 — cluster-olm-operator: add the third component (atomic crossover)
docs.text:
Repo: openshift/cluster-olm-operator. Split into an additive 3a and an atomic crossover 3b.

3a — Plumb the new image reference (only after the image is available in CI). - Add OBJECT_CONTROLLER_IMAGE env var to the operator Deployment (manifests/0000_51_olm_06_deployment.yaml), dev default quay.io/openshift/origin-olm-object-controller:latest. - Add an object-controller entry to manifests/image-references. - Add a copy-object-controller-manifests initContainer (runs the new operand image's cp-manifests). - Ordering gate: 3a references the new operand image (initContainer + image-references). It must merge only after Phase 2 + Phase 0 make the image available in the CI payload, or the operator pod fails to start. - 3a alone does not yet render or deploy object-controller as a separate component, so no behavior change for the operand → green.

3b — Crossover: enable the new render, suppress the old passenger (atomic). - Add "object-controller" to BuildControllers(...). - In helm.go, set options.objectController.deployment.image ← OBJECT_CONTROLLER_IMAGE (for the object-controller render), and keep the operator-controller render from setting it. - Drive object-controller enablement: in the object-controller render, map the BoxcutterRuntime gate → options.objectController.enabled=true only when the gate is on and featureSet is experimental; otherwise the component renders empty. (Per Phase 1, the shipped object-controller.yaml leaves enabled unset, so this runtime set is what actually turns the component on.) - Avoid an idle namespace on GA/non-TechPreview clusters: the empty render still emits the openshift-object-controller namespace + a default-deny NetworkPolicy. Decide whether cluster-olm-operator should skip building/applying the object-controller component entirely when BoxcutterRuntime is off (cleaner), or accept the idle namespace. Prefer skipping. - Suppress the old passenger: in the operator-controller render, set options.objectController.enabled=false (now permitted after upstream U1 is baked into the operand chart) so object-controller no longer renders into openshift-operator-controller. - Add openshift-object-controller namespace handling + RBAC readiness waits; generalize or replace objectControllerRendered() / waitForOLMv1ComponentsRBAC to look in the new namespace. Confirm the operator's own ClusterRole already grants the object-controller role/binding management in the new namespace (it has object-controller-* grants today). - Update e2e expectations to look for object-controller in openshift-object-controller. - Atomicity: the move from openshift-operator-controller → openshift-object-controller happens in one merge — no double-deploy. - Prerequisite: operand images must carry the U1 chart (so objectController.enabled=false is honored by the operator-controller render) — i.e. the fork has rebased past U1 and images are rebuilt. - CI impact: TechPreview e2e now finds object-controller in its own namespace; updated in the same merge → green. Standard (non-TechPreview) e2e unaffected (object-controller renders empty).

docs.title: Phase 4 — Cleanup (the "clean up this repo" PR(s))
docs.text: After 3b is live and verified on all target branches. - Downstream fork: - operator-controller.Dockerfile: stop copying /object-controller. - operator-controller.yaml: remove the objectController block. - Regenerate openshift/operator-controller/manifests*.yaml snapshots. - cluster-olm-operator: remove the old OPERATOR_CONTROLLER_IMAGE-reuse for object-controller and any now-dead detection branches for the old namespace. - cluster-olm-operator (optional hygiene): a best-effort delete of any leftover object-controller Deployment/SA/RBAC in openshift-operator-controller, mirroring the existing hardcoded cleanupOldOperatorControllerRBAC pattern. Not required for correctness (fresh installs never create those objects per §6.5); useful only for dev clusters that manually toggled BoxcutterRuntime. - Upstream: no functional cleanup required — upstream intentionally keeps the dual-mode chart (single-namespace deploy for local/upstream use). Optional: tighten docs. - CI impact: each cleanup is a removal of now-unused behavior; green because nothing consumes the removed paths anymore.

docs.title: 8. Sequencing summary and CI-safety invariants
docs.text:
Phase 0 (ART, external) ─────────────────────────────┐ (image available in CI)
                                                      v
U1/U2/U3 (upstream, additive) → rebase to fork → operand images rebuilt with U1 chart
                                                      │
Phase 1 (fork: new image assets, additive) ──────────┤
                                                      │
Phase 2 (ocp-build-data: image config, additive) ────┤
                                                      v
Phase 3a (c-olm-o: image ref plumbing)  [needs image available]
                                                      v
Phase 3b (c-olm-o: atomic crossover)    [needs U1 chart in operand images]
                                                      v
Phase 4 (cleanup: fork + c-olm-o)       [needs 3b live everywhere]

Invariants checked at every merge: - I1 — no dangling image ref: no repo references OBJECT_CONTROLLER_IMAGE, the object-controller image-references entry, or the copy-object-controller-manifests initContainer until the image is built and available (Phase 0+2 before Phase 3a). - I2 — no double-deploy: the old passenger render is suppressed in the exact same merge that enables the new render (Phase 3b). - I3 — upstream renders unchanged: U1/U2/U3 keep every checked-in manifests/*.yaml byte-identical. - I4 — default clusters unaffected: object-controller only renders under experimental + BoxcutterRuntime throughout; standard renders stay empty.

docs.title: 9. Open items left to the builder
docs.text:
• U1 helper refactor shape: choose the least-invasive _helpers.tpl change satisfying both the standalone-render and the force-exclude requirements while keeping existing manifests unchanged. Validate with make manifests + the new U2 smoke render.
  • Enablement mechanism (Phase 1 vs 3b): decide whether the object-controller component's enablement is driven purely by the shipped object-controller.yaml (enabled: true, relying on experimental overlay) or by cluster-olm-operator setting objectController.enabled at render time based on the BoxcutterRuntime gate. Prefer whichever keeps the standard render empty without a chart error and avoids divergence between the two mechanisms.
  • Target release branches: confirm whether the separation lands on openshift-4.21 only or is also backported to openshift-4.20 (affects ocp-build-data branches and fork release branches).
  • kube-rbac-proxy / metrics: confirm object-controller metrics serving in the new namespace matches operator-controller (cert-manager vs openshift-service-ca, ServiceMonitor, cluster-monitoring namespace label).
  • ClusterOperator relatedObjects / status: confirm the new namespace and object-controller objects are recorded as related objects and that incompatible_operator_controller.go's ClusterObjectSet handling is unaffected by the namespace move.
  • RBAC readiness wait generalization: confirm SCC privileged access and RBAC propagation waits work for the new namespace.
  • CRD render-ownership hardening (optional): decide whether to additionally render the ClusterObjectSet CRD from a stable component to remove the transient start-order race (§6.5), or accept the eventually-consistent default.
  • GA timing (tracking, not a build decision): ensure the split lands before BoxcutterRuntime is promoted to Default (constraint 7). If GA timing slips ahead of the split, the migration assumptions in §6.5 must be revisited.

docs.title: 10. Repos and key files touched
docs.text:
• Upstream — operator-framework/operator-controller (this repo): helm/olmv1/templates/_helpers.tpl, Makefile (manifests smoke target), docs/draft/concepts/clusterobjectsets.md.
  • Downstream fork — openshift/operator-framework-operator-controller: new openshift/object-controller.Dockerfile, openshift/object-controller/cp-manifests, openshift/helm/object-controller.yaml, openshift/helm/generate-manifests.sh, new openshift/object-controller/manifests*.yaml; later openshift/operator-controller.Dockerfile + openshift/helm/operator-controller.yaml.
  • openshift/ocp-build-data: new images/ose-olm-object-controller.yml per target branch.
  • openshift/cluster-olm-operator: manifests/0000_51_olm_06_deployment.yaml, manifests/image-references, pkg/controller/helm.go, pkg/controller/builder.go, cmd/cluster-olm-operator/main.go, internal/featuregates/mapper.go / pkg/controller/featuregates_hook.go, e2e. ```

docs.title: ClusterObjectDeployment Controller MVP — Design
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-20 Status: approved for planning Branch: cod-controller-mvp (off cod-controller-skeleton, PR #3032)

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Give the ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) controller its first real behavior. Today it is a skeleton (PR #3032): it watches COD + owned ClusterObjectSet (COS) but does nothing. This MVP makes it roll out template changes as new COS revisions and report rollout progress.

The COD lives in the object-controller binary, is experimental-only (//go:build !standard, experimental-channel CRD), and reuses the existing COS sub-types verbatim.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. On a detected template change (or when no revision exists), create a new COS revision owned by the COD.
  2. Reflect the latest revision's rollout progress in the COD's single Progressing condition.

docs.title: Non-goals (handled elsewhere or deferred)
docs.text:
• Archival / supersession of older revisions — done today by the COS controller (clusterobjectset_controller.go:325, TODO(COD)); not moved in this MVP.
  • Progress deadlines — a COS concern; the cut-down COD CRD has no deadline field.
  • Pruning / revision-history limits — the cut-down COD CRD has no limit field.
  • Orphan adoption — the group→COD watch exists (skeleton) but COD only manages COS it creates.
  • Object externalization to Secrets — the applier does this for bundle content; COD copies user-authored template phases verbatim (inline objects stay inline).

docs.title: Key facts (from recon)
docs.text:
• COD CRD is cut down. Spec.Template.Spec = {Phases, ProgressionProbes, CollisionProtection} (no template metadata). Status = {Conditions} only. Condition type Progressing; reasons NewClusterObjectSetProgressed / NewClusterObjectSetProgressing (constants already defined in api/v1/clusterobjectdeployment_types.go). COD name is a valid COS group (≤52 chars).
  • COS sub-types are identical to the COD template's, so BuildCOS is a direct typed field copy.
  • Revision ancestry is runtime-derived, not stored: all COS sharing spec.group form the ordered sequence (sort by spec.revision). There is no Previous field. spec.group has a field index registered by controllers.SetupIndexes (already wired in main.go).
  • COS readiness/completion: status.completedAt (set-once, immutable) marks "rolled out". The live Ready condition is True/AllObjectsReady when ready. This repo's own GetRevisionStates uses completedAt for "Installed"; the COD uses it the same way.
  • Naming: child COS name = <cod-name>-<revision> (matches applier convention).
  • Owner labels on COS: olm.operatorframework.io/owner-kind + owner-name (internal/shared/labels).

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Change detection: template-hash label (orb-style), not SSA-diff. Compute a SHA-256 over the marshaled cod.Spec.Template, store a truncated hex digest as a label on each COS, and compare the latest active COS's label to the current hash. Chosen because it honors the CRD contract "any template change → new revision" (the SSA-diff approach silently mutates a revision on a change to a mutable COS field such as progressionProbes), is self-contained, and is unit- testable with the fake client. New label constant: olm.operatorframework.io/template-hash. Digest truncated to 32 hex chars (sha256[:16]) to stay within the 63-char label-value limit.
  • Create mechanism: plain typed Client.Create (not SSA). Revisions are immutable and the controller only ever creates them; AlreadyExists is treated as success (requeue race).
  • Completion signal: COS status.completedAt (not the live Ready condition) so a later availability regression does not un-complete the rollout.
  • No finalizer. COS children are cleaned up by Kubernetes cascading delete via the controller owner reference.

docs.title: Reconcile (outer)
docs.text: Get the COD (ignore not-found). If DeletionTimestamp is set, no-op (children cascade). Deep-copy, run the inner reconcile, and if Status changed, write it via the status subresource, joining any update error.

docs.title: reconcile (inner)
docs.text:
1. List COS in the group (cod.Name) via the .spec.group index; sort ascending by spec.revision.
  2. hash = templateHash(cod.Spec.Template).
  3. latest = latestActiveRevision(revs) — highest-revision COS that is not Archived and not deleting.
  4. If latest == nil or latest.Labels[template-hash] != hash: create a new revision (nextRevision = max(revision over all revs)+1), then set Progressing=True / NewClusterObjectSetProgressing ("waiting for new revision to be created").
  5. Else (latest matches current template):
  6. completedAt set → Progressing=False / NewClusterObjectSetProgressed ("latest revision has progressed").
  7. else → Progressing=True / NewClusterObjectSetProgressing ("latest revision is progressing").

Requeues are driven by the existing Owns(COS) watch (COS status changes re-trigger the COD); no timer.

docs.title: BuildCOS
docs.text: Name <cod>-<rev>; labels owner-kind=ClusterObjectDeployment, owner-name=<cod>, template-hash=<hash>; spec group=<cod>, revision=<rev>, lifecycleState=Active, phases/progressionProbes copied from template, collisionProtection from template defaulting to Prevent when empty; controller owner reference to the COD (needs a Scheme on the reconciler).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Unit (fake client + .spec.group index via testutil.WithIndexes): create-first-revision, no-op-when-hash-matches (completed → Progressing False; not-completed → Progressing True), new-revision-on-template-change, new-revision-when-latest-archived, deletion no-op; plus pure- function tests for hash determinism/sensitivity, BuildCOS field mapping, collisionProtection default, nextRevision, latestActiveRevision.
  • E2E (test/e2e/features/cod_rollout.feature, @BoxcutterRuntime, experimental cluster): initial rollout → COD Progressing False; template change → revision 2 ready → Progressing False; unchanged template → no revision 2. Requires a new Godog step asserting a condition directly on a ClusterObjectDeployment.

docs.title: Out-of-repo-convention notes
docs.text: The ClusterExtension applier uses SSA-diff for change detection and externalizes objects to Secrets; COD intentionally diverges (hash label, inline copy) for MVP simplicity. The applier is itself marked TODO(COD) for eventual replacement, so COD is free to define its own clean mechanism.

docs.title: Design: operator-controller delegates revision management to ClusterObjectDeployment
docs.text:
• Status: Draft (for review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Branch: operator-controller-use-cod (built on main + #3050 progressDeadlineMinutes + #3052 revisionHistoryLimit)

docs.title: Intent & why
docs.text:
Today the operator-controller's ClusterExtension controller manages the entire ClusterObjectSet (COS) revision lifecycle itself: it computes the desired revision, diffs it, creates each COS, packs objects into Secrets, patches owner references, and garbage-collects old revisions. Meanwhile a separate ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) controller already exists in the object-controller binary that is purpose-built to manage COS revisions for a deployment template.

The two code paths overlap and duplicate revision mechanics (both independently build and create COS objects today). The goal of this refactor is an architectural separation of concerns: make the COD the single owner of COS revision lifecycle, and shrink the operator-controller to rendering desired content and writing one COD per ClusterExtension. This is the direction the existing TODO(COD) markers in internal/operator-controller/applier/boxcutter.go and internal/object-controller/controllers/clusterobjectset_controller.go point toward.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• operator-controller creates and maintains exactly one COD per ClusterExtension (COD name == ext.Name == COS spec.group), instead of creating COS revisions directly.
  • The COD controller is the single component that creates, archives, retains, and rolls out COS revisions.
  • ClusterExtension status (Installed, Available, Progressing, .status.install) is derived from the COD (single source of truth for rollout state), plus operator-controller's own pre-apply error reporting.
  • Existing installations continue to work across the upgrade:
  • Helm-based installs migrate to a COD (Helm → COD), which then produces revision 1.
  • Pre-existing COS revisions (created by the current operator-controller) are adopted by the new COD without a disruptive re-rollout.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Changing the COS API or the COS controller's reconcile semantics (archival, probes, collision protection, progress deadline) beyond what is explicitly called out here.
  • Moving archival of predecessor revisions from the COS controller to the COD controller. That remains a separate TODO(COD) and is out of scope; the COS controller continues to archive its lower-numbered siblings on completion.
  • Enriching the COD Progressing condition with the finer COS-level rollout reasons (Retrying/Blocked). We explicitly accept coarser rollout reasons (see Decisions).
  • Changing deprecation status handling (it is derived from the catalog, not from revisions, and is unaffected).

docs.title: Anti-goals (what would make this a failure)
docs.text:
• Any window in which ClusterExtension.status.install.bundle reports a bundle that has not actually rolled out (this corrupts upgrade-path resolution).
  • An upgrade that re-rolls or disrupts a healthy, already-installed workload because the new COD does not recognize existing revisions.
  • Secret objects leaking (never garbage collected) or being deleted while still referenced by a live revision.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Experimental-only; standard behaviour is frozen. All changes are confined to the BoxcutterRuntime feature-gated code path. The gate is enabled only in the experimental manifest (manifests/experimental.yaml), not the standard one (cmd/operator-controller/main.go selects applier.Boxcutter + BoxcutterRevisionStatesGetter + BoxcutterStorageMigrator when the gate is on, and the Helm applier + HelmRevisionStatesGetter when it is off). COS/COD are experimental APIs.
  • No standard-manifest e2e may change. e2e scenarios that run against the standard manifest set must not be modified and must pass unchanged. Only experimental e2es (and @BoxcutterRuntime-tagged features) may change behaviour or assertions. Behaviour changes are permitted only on the experimental API path.
  • The Helm/standard status path is untouched. The HelmRevisionStatesGetter path and the observable CE conditions/reasons it produces must remain byte-for-byte equivalent. The new COD-based status derivation is a separate, gated path — it must not be implemented by mutating the shared common_controller.go helpers in a way that changes the Helm path's output. (Consequence: the "accept coarser Progressing reasons" and "wedged rollout never shows Failed" decisions apply only to the experimental path; the standard path keeps its current reasons.)

docs.title: Background: current state (verified against the tree)
operator-controller applier (internal/operator-controller/applier/boxcutter.go)
docs.text:
• Boxcutter.Apply lists existing COS by group (revisions.ListForGroup, group = ext.Name), generates the desired COS, SSA-diffs refs-vs-refs to classify install/upgrade/unchanged, runs preflights, creates the COS with objects externalized to Secrets, patches Secret owner refs → COS UID, and garbage-collects archived revisions beyond a limit.
  • SimpleRevisionGenerator builds the COS (buildClusterObjectSet), sets collision protection (Prevent normal, None for Helm-migrated), progression probes, and progress-deadline passthrough.
  • BoxcutterStorageMigrator.Migrate creates revision 1 directly from a deployed Helm release, marks it CompletedAt, labelled MigratedFromHelmKey.

docs.title: Secret packing (internal/operator-controller/applier/secretpacker.go)
docs.text: • Already essentially content-addressable: Secret data keys are content hashes (contentHash); Secret name is <RevisionName>-<hash-of-data> (secretNameFromData). The only revision coupling is the RevisionName prefix and the RevisionNameKey label. Secrets are immutable, typed labels.SecretTypeObjectData, in the system namespace.

docs.title: COD controller (internal/object-controller/controllers/clusterobjectdeployment_controller.go)
docs.text:
• For(COD).Owns(COS) plus a Watches mapping COS spec.group → COD name, which adopts not-yet-owned (orphan) COS in the group.
  • Creates the next revision when the latest active revision's TemplateHashKey label != templateHash(spec.template); copies Phases, ProgressDeadlineMinutes, ProgressionProbes, CollisionProtection verbatim into the COS.
  • setAvailable: True/Available if any active (non-archived, non-deleting) revision is COS Ready; else False/Unavailable or False/NoActiveRevision.
  • Progressing: True/NewClusterObjectSetProgressing while rolling, False/NewClusterObjectSetProgressed on completion (latest.Status.CompletedAt), False/ProgressDeadlineExceeded on deadline breach. setCondition stamps ObservedGeneration = cod.Generation.
  • Retention/GC landed in #3052 (garbageCollectArchivedRevisions), keyed by spec.revisionHistoryLimit.

docs.title: CE status derivation (internal/operator-controller/controllers/)
docs.text:
• BoxcutterRevisionStatesGetter.GetRevisionStates lists COS by group, skips archived, classifies a revision Installed when Status.CompletedAt != 0 (its bundle metadata → .status.install.bundle) and RollingOut otherwise.
  • Bundle metadata is read from COS annotations: package-name, bundle-name, bundle-version, bundle-release, bundle-reference (internal/shared/labels/labels.go).
  • common_controller.go maps: Available from the installed revision's COS Ready (re-emitted ProbesSucceeded); Installed True/Succeeded when a completed revision exists, else False/Absent|Failed; Progressing from the latest rolling revision's COS Ready.Reason → RollingOut/Retrying/Blocked/ ProgressDeadlineExceeded/Succeeded, and from operator-controller's own pre-apply errors (setStatusProgressing: Retrying/Blocked/InvalidConfiguration).

docs.title: Target architecture
docs.text:
ClusterExtension (operator-controller)
  ├─ resolve bundle (catalog)            ── unchanged
  ├─ unpack content                      ── unchanged
  ├─ render manifests                    ── unchanged
  ├─ run preflights (CRD safety)         ── STAYS in operator-controller
  ├─ pack objects into Secrets           ── STAYS in operator-controller (content-addressed, COD-owned)
  └─ SSA write ONE ClusterObjectDeployment  ── REPLACES direct COS creation
        (template = ref'd phases, + bundle-metadata annotations)
            │
            ▼
ClusterObjectDeployment (object-controller)   ── single owner of revision lifecycle
  ├─ create next COS revision (verbatim template)
  ├─ retention / GC (revisionHistoryLimit)     ── #3052
  ├─ progress deadline                         ── #3050
  └─ status: Available, Progressing (+ ObservedGeneration)
            │
            ▼
ClusterObjectSet (object-controller)          ── unchanged; archives its own predecessors

docs.title: 1. operator-controller writes a COD instead of COS revisions
docs.text:
Boxcutter.Apply is refactored to: 1. Render the desired objects (unchanged ManifestProvider / SimpleRevisionGenerator logic that produces phases). 2. Run preflights (unchanged). 3. Pack objects into content-addressed Secrets (see §2). 4. Build a COD apply configuration with: - spec.template.spec = the ref'd phases + progressionProbes + collisionProtection + progressDeadlineMinutes (the fields that used to go on the COS now go on the template; COD copies them to each COS). - metadata.annotations = bundle-metadata annotations (see §4/§5). - owner reference → the ClusterExtension. 5. Server-side apply the COD (field owner unchanged). The COD controller does the rest (revision creation, archival via COS, retention, rollout).

The direct COS mechanics removed from operator-controller: createExternalizedRevision, garbageCollectOldRevisions, latestRevisionNumber, revision SSA-diff/state machine, Secret owner-ref patching to the COS. Secret packing stays.

collisionProtection today is Prevent for normal installs and None for Helm-migrated. On the COD template it is a single value per COD; see §5 for how the Helm-migration None case is handled.

docs.title: 2. Secret packing & ownership
docs.text:
• Keying: drop the per-revision RevisionName prefix from the Secret name; prefix with the extension/COD name instead (e.g. <ext.Name>-<content-hash>). Data keys remain content hashes. Secrets become fully content-addressed and revision-number-independent, so operator-controller can create them without knowing the revision number the COD will assign.
  • Ownership: operator-controller sets the Secret owner reference to the ClusterExtension. The CE object is already in hand during reconcile, so no COD/COS UID lookup or two-phase owner-ref patch is needed, and it is consistent with the COD itself being CE-owned. Secrets cascade-delete when the ClusterExtension is deleted.
  • References: the COD template carries ObjectSourceRefs pointing at these Secrets; the COD controller copies them verbatim into each COS (buildClusterObjectSet already copies Phases as-is), and the COS controller resolves them unchanged.
  • Secret GC (builder decision, see Open Items): because Secrets are CE-owned (not COS-owned), deleting an archived COS during retention does not cascade to its Secrets, and old-content Secrets accumulate as the template changes over the CE's lifetime. A pruning pass must delete Secrets in the group that are no longer referenced by any live COS revision (active or retained-archived). Content addressing makes this safe: a Secret shared by multiple revisions is retained while any revision references it. Recommended home: the COD controller (it already owns revision GC and can enumerate every revision's refs; it can delete the Secrets regardless of their owner). This must run after retention GC and must never delete a Secret referenced by a not-yet-GC'd archived revision.
  • Creation ordering: operator-controller creates the Secrets (owner ref = CE, set directly — the CE exists) before applying the COD. Because the COD controller then asynchronously creates a COS referencing those Secrets, there is a brief window where a COS may reference a Secret that is already present (Secrets created first) — the ordering (Secrets → COD) avoids a dangling ref, and the COS controller's normal resolve-with-retry covers any transient lag. CE-ownership removes the old two-phase owner-ref patch entirely (no COD/COS UID needed first).
  • Deletion ordering (risk): with CE-ownership, Secret deletion is driven by the CE's deletion rather than each COS's. The design must ensure referenced Secrets outlive any COS teardown that still needs to resolve them (e.g. via the CE finalizer ordering, so the COD/COS teardown completes before the CE — and thus its Secrets — is garbage collected).

docs.title: 3. Preflights stay in operator-controller
docs.text:
CRD-safety Install/Upgrade preflights run in Boxcutter.Apply before the COD is written, exactly as today. A preflight failure is surfaced on the CE Progressing condition via the existing pre-apply error path (§4) and the COD is not updated.

Install-vs-Upgrade selection (builder call): today the choice between preflight.Install and preflight.Upgrade is produced by the COS SSA-diff state machine (boxcutter.go StateNeedsInstall/StateNeedsUpgrade), which §1 removes. Replacement signal: treat it as an Install when the extension has no prior completed revision, else an Upgrade — derivable without reading COS from either (a) the existence of the COD / whether it has ever reported Progressing=False/NewClusterObjectSetProgressed, or (b) the CE's own current .status.install (populated == already installed). Recommended: key off the CE's .status.install presence, falling back to a COD Get when status is empty, so no COS read is reintroduced. This is the one piece of "current state" operator-controller still inspects before writing the COD.

docs.title: 4. ClusterExtension status (COD as single source of truth)
docs.text:
CE status is derived on the success path from the COD, and on the error path from operator-controller's own reconcile errors (unchanged). Concretely:

  • Available — mirror COD.Available onto CE.Available. COD reports True while any active revision is Ready, which preserves availability across upgrades. Reason mapping: builder decision — either adopt COD's reasons (Available/Unavailable/NoActiveRevision) or re-map to CE's existing ProbesSucceeded for API compatibility (recommended: re-map True → ProbesSucceeded to minimize client-visible change; pass through the non-ready states).
  • Progressing — layered:
  • If operator-controller hits a pre-apply error (resolution, unpack, preflight), set Progressing from that error as today (Retrying/Blocked/InvalidConfiguration). The COD is not written.
  • Otherwise (a valid COD was applied), derive Progressing from COD.Progressing. We accept the coarser reasons: COD's NewClusterObjectSetProgressing / NewClusterObjectSetProgressed / ProgressDeadlineExceeded. The finer COS-level Retrying/Blocked rollout reasons are intentionally not preserved on the success path.
  • Accepted status regression (revisit in a future PR): because COD does not surface the COS Ready reasons (ObjectCollision/PreconditionsNotMet/ InvalidSpecification), a rollout wedged on one of those shows Progressing=True/RollingOut and Installed=False/Absent — never Failed — until the progress deadline eventually flips Progressing to False/ProgressDeadlineExceeded. This is accepted for now (consistent with the coarser-reasons decision) and will be revisited (likely by enriching COD) in a follow-up.
  • Installed + .status.install — update only when the COD reports the current rollout complete:
  • Condition: COD.Progressing.Status == False and COD.Progressing.Reason == NewClusterObjectSetProgressed and COD.Progressing.ObservedGeneration == COD.metadata.generation (the generation gate, see §5). When satisfied, set Installed=True/Succeeded and populate .status.install.bundle from the COD's bundle-metadata annotations.
  • When the gate is not satisfied, hold the previous .status.install (latch behaviour across upgrades). Only clear it / set Installed=False when there has never been a completed revision — detectable via COD.Available == False/NoActiveRevision together with no prior install.

On the BoxcutterRuntime path only, BoxcutterRevisionStatesGetter and the COS-reading status derivation (boxcutter_reconcile_steps.go) are replaced by a COD-reading equivalent, and the CE controller no longer lists or reads COS objects. The HelmRevisionStatesGetter path (standard manifest) and any shared common_controller.go helpers it relies on are left untouched; the COD-based derivation must be added as a separate, gated path rather than by changing the Helm path's observable output.

docs.title: 5. Bundle-metadata annotations on the COD + generation gate
docs.text:
• operator-controller sets annotations on the COD reflecting the desired bundle: package-name, bundle-name, bundle-version, bundle-release, bundle-reference (reusing the existing keys in internal/shared/labels/labels.go). It writes these in the same apply as spec.template.
  • Annotations, not labels: several of these values are not label-safe — bundle-reference is an image ref (registry/foo@sha256:..., contains //:/@, exceeds 63 chars) and bundle-version may carry build metadata (1.0.0+2, contains +). They are COS annotations today for exactly this reason. Annotations, like labels, are metadata and do not bump generation, so the gate below is unaffected.
  • The two-writer race: the annotations are written by operator-controller; Progressing is written by the COD controller. Between operator-controller applying a new template+annotations and the COD controller reconciling, COD.Progressing can still read False/NewClusterObjectSetProgressed from the previous rollout while the annotations already describe the new bundle. Copying annotations → .status.install in that window would report the new bundle as installed before it rolled out.
  • The gate: CE trusts the annotations only when COD.Progressing.ObservedGeneration == COD.metadata.generation. A bundle change always changes rendered content (object annotations carry the bundle version), hence changes spec.template, hence bumps metadata.generation. The COD controller stamps ObservedGeneration on the Progressing condition only after it has reconciled the new generation. So in the race window the condition still carries the old generation and CE correctly waits.
  • The builder-check verified the gate holds against the current COD controller: any generation bump not matched by a template-hash change still routes through the create-revision path and sets Progressing=True before stamping the new ObservedGeneration, so the gate cannot falsely pass.
  • Helm-migration collisionProtection: see §6 for the None → Prevent flip. The COD template value starts None (to adopt Helm-owned objects) and is flipped to Prevent by operator-controller after the first successful rollout.

docs.title: 6. Migration & adoption
docs.text:
• Helm → COD: BoxcutterStorageMigrator is adapted to create a COD (not a COS) from a deployed Helm release. The COD's template starts with collisionProtection: None to adopt the objects the Helm release already owns, and the migrated COD is marked with a pending-flip label (see below). The COD controller then creates revision 1. The "mark revision 1 as completed immediately" behaviour that exists today (so the extension is treated as installed during the upgrade window) must be reproduced: because status is now COD-derived, the migrator (or COD) must ensure the migrated revision records CompletedAt and the COD surfaces Progressing=False/Progressed + bundle annotations, so CE reports the prior bundle as installed without re-rolling.
  • collisionProtection: None → Prevent flip. The per-revision behaviour today — migrated rev 1 is None, every revision after is Prevent — cannot be expressed directly because the COD template is single-valued. It is reproduced as an explicit flip driven by operator-controller:
  • The migrator creates the COD with collisionProtection: None and a pending-flip label (e.g. olm.operatorframework.io/migrated-collision-flip: "true").
  • While the label is present and the COD has not yet reported a successful rollout for the current generation (generation gate, §5), operator-controller keeps the desired template at None (does not flip, avoiding a premature rev 2 before rev 1 is healthy).
  • Once the COD reports Progressing=False/NewClusterObjectSetProgressed for the current generation, operator-controller sets the desired template collisionProtection: Prevent and removes the pending-flip label. This is a template change, so the COD creates a Prevent rev 2 that hands over rev 1's objects.
  • This reproduces proven behaviour. The current architecture already performs the None → Prevent transition across successive same-group revisions (migrated rev 1 None via GenerateRevisionFromHelmRelease, then Prevent via GenerateRevision); the hand-over works because collision protection guards against foreign owners, not a predecessor revision in the same group. The only new machinery is the label-driven, rollout-gated flip of the single template value. Fresh (non-migrated) installs use Prevent from the start and never carry the label.
  • Existing COS adoption: when the new operator-controller writes a COD named ext.Name, the COD controller's group watch adopts the pre-existing COS revisions in that group (sets the controller owner ref). If the latest existing revision's TemplateHashKey matches the COD template hash, no new revision is created and the workload is not disrupted; otherwise a normal rollout of the newly-desired template occurs (the same as any upgrade). The migrator must stamp the TemplateHashKey consistently so a steady-state extension does not trigger a spurious revision on first adoption.

docs.title: 7. Retention / archival (already handled / unchanged)
docs.text:
• Retention/GC: COD (revisionHistoryLimit, #3052).
  • Archival of predecessors: COS controller, unchanged (out of scope to move).

docs.title: What is removed from operator-controller
docs.text:
• Direct COS creation and the install/upgrade/unchanged state machine in Boxcutter.Apply.
  • garbageCollectOldRevisions, latestRevisionNumber, createExternalizedRevision.
  • COS-based status reading (BoxcutterRevisionStatesGetter, the COS Ready→CE mapping helpers), replaced by COD-based reading.
  • Secret owner-ref patching to the COS (Secrets now CE-owned, set directly at creation — no two-phase patch).

Kept: manifest rendering, preflights, Secret packing.

docs.title: Feature gating & rollout
docs.text: COD is an experimental API; this work lands behind the experimental manifest. The standard (non-experimental) path is unaffected until COD graduates. The upgrade from a prior experimental operator-controller to this one must exercise the adoption path (§6) in test/upgrade-e2e.

docs.title: Runtime dependencies & RBAC (builder work)
docs.text:
• New cross-binary status dependency. The COD controller lives in the separate object-controller binary; CE/applier/migrator live in operator-controller. After this change, CE status (Installed/Available/Progressing) depends on the object-controller binary being running (today only workload apply depends on the COS controller). The experimental manifest must guarantee object-controller is deployed wherever operator-controller runs; if the object-controller is down, CE status will not progress. (Note: per project direction the object-controller is being split into its own image/namespace — the manifest/RBAC work here must track that split.)
  • RBAC. operator-controller currently has RBAC for clusterobjectsets but not clusterobjectdeployments. It must gain create;get;list;watch;update;patch (and delete for cleanup) on clusterobjectdeployments, plus continued Secret permissions. COS create/patch RBAC on operator-controller can be dropped once it no longer creates COS.
  • Upgrade ordering. The §6 adoption path must be validated across a cross-binary upgrade (old operator-controller that created COS directly → new one that writes a COD) in test/upgrade-e2e.

docs.title: Testing strategy
docs.text:
• Unit: applier writes the expected COD (template, labels, owner ref, refs); CE status derivation from COD conditions + generation gate (installed only on Progressed + matching ObservedGeneration; held otherwise); secret keying is revision-independent and content-addressed.
  • envtest: COD apply + adoption of pre-existing COS by group; no spurious revision when template hash matches.
  • e2e (experimental only): install → status reports installed bundle; upgrade → .status.install holds the old bundle until the new rollout completes, then flips; Helm → COD migration; availability stays True across an upgrade; secret GC leaves no orphans after retention; the None → Prevent collision flip after migration. New/changed scenarios are @BoxcutterRuntime-tagged and run on the experimental manifest.
  • Standard e2es are not modified and must pass unchanged (the Helm path is untouched). This is a hard acceptance gate for the work.

docs.title: Open items / builder decisions
docs.text:
1. Secret GC home & algorithm (§2) — recommended: a pruning pass in the COD controller that deletes group Secrets unreferenced by any live revision, run after retention GC. Must be proven safe against archived-but-retained revisions.
  2. Available reason mapping (§4) — recommended: re-map COD True → ProbesSucceeded for client compatibility; otherwise adopt COD reasons.
  3. Migrated-revision "installed" signalling (§6) — the exact mechanism by which a Helm→COD migrated install reports installed without re-rolling (reproducing today's immediate-CompletedAt behaviour through the COD).
  4. TemplateHashKey parity on adoption (§6) — ensure the hash operator-controller would compute for a steady-state extension matches the existing revision's label, so adoption does not trigger a spurious rollout. ```

docs.title: Design: ClusterObjectDeployment template metadata propagation
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-23 Status: Draft (pending approval) Branch (to be created): cod-template-metadata (off main)

docs.title: Intent and why
docs.text:
We want a generic, OLM-agnostic way for a ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) to carry labels and annotations down to every ClusterObjectSet (COS) revision it creates — the Kubernetes Deployment.spec.template.metadata → Pod pattern, matching orb-operator's ClusterObjectDeploymentTemplateMetadata.

Why now / the motivating problem: on the operator-controller-use-cod branch, the COD controller hardcodes a list of OLM-specific annotation keys (bundleAnnotationKeys: package-name, bundle-*, olm.properties) and copies them from the COD's top-level ObjectMeta onto each COS, so the ClusterExtension status reader (which reads bundle metadata off each COS) keeps working. That hardcoded list is an OLM concept leaking into a controller that is meant to be generic.

Scope decision (set by the human): build the generic capability on main as a self-contained change. Leave operator-controller-use-cod untouched. That branch will later adopt this capability — replacing bundleAnnotationKeys with populating template.metadata — as follow-up work on that branch, not here.

This keeps the main change pure infrastructure with zero OLM knowledge, which is exactly the boundary we want.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Add a generic spec.template.metadata (labels + annotations) to the COD API.
  • Propagate those labels/annotations verbatim onto each COS revision the COD controller creates, with the controller-managed template-hash label taking precedence.
  • Keep the change additive and OLM-agnostic: no knowledge of bundles anywhere in the COD controller.
  • Match orb-operator semantics so the implementations stay convergent.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Removing bundleAnnotationKeys or changing the operator-controller applier — those live on operator-controller-use-cod and are follow-ups on that branch, not part of this PR.
  • Changing where/how the CE reads revision state.
  • Adding per-revision history to COD status.
  • Any change to COS behavior, phases, or rollout logic.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• Do not introduce any OLM concept into the COD controller.
  • Do not let callers override controller-managed revision machinery (the template-hash label) via template.metadata.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• api/v1/*_types.go changes follow OpenShift + Kubernetes API conventions (AGENTS.md): value types with omitzero/omitempty, +optional, doc comments using lowercase JSON field names. Run make generate manifests crd-ref-docs and make lint-api-diff.
  • The COD API is experimental; incompatible changes are allowed.
  • olm.operatorframework.io/* prefixes stay in the OLM domain (AGENTS.md). The template-hash label keeps that prefix — it is COD machinery, not a bundle concept — and remains controller-managed.
  • Must build/pass on macOS and Linux.

docs.title: 1. API change (api/v1/clusterobjectdeployment_types.go)
docs.text:
Add a Metadata field to ClusterObjectDeploymentTemplate and a new type:

// ClusterObjectDeploymentTemplate describes the caller-controlled part of a revision.
type ClusterObjectDeploymentTemplate struct {
    // metadata contains labels and annotations propagated verbatim to each
    // ClusterObjectSet created from this template. Changes to metadata change
    // template identity and therefore create a new revision.
    // +optional
    Metadata ClusterObjectDeploymentTemplateMetadata `json:"metadata,omitzero"`

    // spec contains the desired revision content. Group, revision, lifecycle state,
    // and ownership are assigned by the controller and cannot be set here.
    // +required
    Spec ClusterObjectDeploymentTemplateSpec `json:"spec,omitzero"`
}

// ClusterObjectDeploymentTemplateMetadata contains labels and annotations
// propagated to each ClusterObjectSet revision created from the template.
type ClusterObjectDeploymentTemplateMetadata struct {
    // labels is a set of key/value pairs propagated to each revision's metadata.
    // +optional
    // +kubebuilder:validation:MaxProperties=32
    Labels map[string]string `json:"labels,omitempty"`

    // annotations is a set of key/value pairs propagated to each revision's
    // metadata. Each value must be 256 KiB or less.
    // +optional
    // +kubebuilder:validation:MaxProperties=32
    // +kubebuilder:validation:XValidation:rule="self.all(k, size(self[k]) <= 262144)",message="annotation values must be 256 KiB or less"
    Annotations map[string]string `json:"annotations,omitempty"`
}

Regeneration: make generate manifests crd-ref-docs updates zz_generated.deepcopy.go, applyconfigurations under applyconfigurations/api/v1/, the standard/experimental CRDs, the manifests, and the API reference docs. Validate with make lint-api-diff.

TemplateHash already hashes the whole ClusterObjectDeploymentTemplate via hashutil.DeepHashObject, which is JSON-based (json.Encoder → sha224). Adding Metadata folds it into template identity automatically: a change to metadata (once set) produces a different hash and cuts a new revision. No hashing code changes. Because the field is omitzero, a COD that sets no metadata serializes exactly as before, so existing CODs keep the same hash (see Compatibility).

docs.title: 2. COD controller (internal/object-controller/controllers/clusterobjectdeployment_controller.go)
docs.text:
buildClusterObjectSet on main today sets only the template-hash label and no annotations. Extend it to propagate cod.Spec.Template.Metadata:

  • Labels: clone Metadata.Labels, then set labels.TemplateHashKey = hash last so the controller-managed hash label always wins over a caller-supplied value of the same key.
  • Annotations: clone Metadata.Annotations verbatim (nil → no annotations).

Sketch:

revLabels := maps.Clone(cod.Spec.Template.Metadata.Labels)
if revLabels == nil {
    revLabels = map[string]string{}
}
revLabels[labels.TemplateHashKey] = hash

return &ocv1.ClusterObjectSet{
    ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{
        Name:        fmt.Sprintf("%s-%d", cod.Name, revision),
        Labels:      revLabels,
        Annotations: maps.Clone(cod.Spec.Template.Metadata.Annotations),
    },
    Spec: ...unchanged...,
}

docs.title: Propagation / merge semantics (decided)
docs.text:
• Controller-managed keys win. Only template-hash is controller-managed; it is applied after cloning Metadata.Labels, overwriting any caller value.
  • No validation rejecting caller use of reserved keys — the controller overwrites. Keeps the controller simple and generic.
  • Nil maps tolerated.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• Experimental API; no migration guarantees.
  • metadata is omitzero and DeepHashObject is JSON-based, so a COD that sets no metadata hashes identically to before this change. No re-rollout churn for existing CODs on main.
  • The upgrade re-rollout churn discussed during design (existing CODs getting one content-identical new revision because annotations move into the hashed template) only arises when template.metadata is actually populated — i.e. on operator-controller-use-cod when operator-controller starts writing bundle annotations there. That is handled on that branch, out of scope here.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• COD controller unit tests (follow existing table-test conventions):
  • template.metadata.labels/annotations are propagated verbatim onto created COSes.
  • a caller-supplied template-hash label is overridden by the controller.
  • a metadata-only template change produces a different hash and cuts a new revision; empty metadata leaves the hash unchanged (no churn).
  • api/v1/validation_test.go: add cases for MaxProperties / the annotation-value size rule if warranted.
  • Full ./internal/object-controller/... suite; make verify, make lint, make test-unit.
  • e2e (experimental suite — COD is experimental): a focused scenario that creates a COD with spec.template.metadata labels + annotations and asserts the created COS revision carries them, plus that the controller-managed template-hash label is present (not clobbered). This exercises what unit tests cannot: the CRD schema accepting the new field through a real apiserver (including the MaxProperties / 256 KiB validation) and propagation end-to-end. Reuse the existing steps ClusterObjectSet "<name>" has label "<key>" with value "<value>" (ClusterObjectSetHasLabelWithValue) and ClusterObjectSet "<name>" contains annotation "<key>" with value (ClusterObjectSetHasAnnotationWithValue) — no new step defs required. Natural home: test/e2e/features/cod_rollout.feature or a small dedicated cod_template_metadata.feature. Run via make test-experimental-e2e.

docs.title: Decisions made (my calls, flagged for review)
docs.text:
• Scope is additive and main-based. Removal of bundleAnnotationKeys and the operator-controller applier change are explicitly deferred to the operator-controller-use-cod branch.
  • Metadata participates in the hash (metadata-only change → new revision), matching orb and K8s; omitzero means existing metadata-less CODs are unaffected.
  • Field shape mirrors orb: Metadata{Labels, Annotations}, no name.
  • MaxProperties=32 on both maps and the 256 KiB per-annotation-value CEL bound, both matching orb.
  • template-hash stays controller-managed and overrides caller values.

docs.title: Follow-up (on operator-controller-use-cod, not this PR)
docs.text:
Once this capability is on main and the branch rebases onto it:

  1. Delete bundleAnnotationKeys and the top-level annotation copy from the COD controller.
  2. Change the operator-controller applier (internal/operator-controller/applier/clusterobjectdeployment.go) to write the bundle annotations into spec.template.metadata.annotations instead of the COD top-level ObjectMeta.
  3. Accept (or explicitly handle) the one-time content-identical re-rollout per installed ClusterExtension that results from the annotations moving into the hashed template.

docs.title: What's left to the builder
docs.text:
• Exact kubebuilder marker tuning to satisfy make lint-api-diff (incl. the CEL rule syntax).
  • maps.Clone vs. an existing helper.
  • Test-table structure, following existing COD controller test conventions.

docs.title: Design: ClusterObjectDeployment / ClusterObjectSet referenced-secret ownership
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-24 Status: Draft (pending approval) Branch: cod-cos-secret-ownership (off main)

docs.title: Intent and why
docs.text:
ClusterObjectSet (COS) phases can reference serialized object manifests stored in Secrets (ObjectSourceRef{name, namespace, key}), and OLM packs rendered bundle content into immutable, content-addressed Secrets of type olm.operatorframework.io/object-data. We need a clear, self-contained rule for who owns those Secrets and when they get deleted, so that content Secrets do not leak across upgrades, revision churn, or deletion — while keeping the ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) and COS usable on their own, outside any ClusterExtension (CE).

Why now / the motivating problem: on the operator-controller-use-cod branch, ownership of packed Secrets was moved onto the ClusterExtension, which is long-lived and never drops ownership. A code review found that this leaks Secrets: once content changes across an upgrade, the old content's Secrets are never referenced by a live revision again and are never deleted until the CE itself is removed. We want an ownership model whose lifetime is scoped to the things that actually consume the content (the COS revisions), not to the CE.

Scope decision (set by the human): this design covers only the object-controller side — COD and COS. The CE / operator-controller side (who creates the Secrets and how it bridges the pre-COS window) is deferred and captured here only as a contract the creator must honor.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• A referenced Secret's lifecycle follows the COS(es) that reference it: it is deleted once no live COS references it.
  • No leaks across revision churn, COD deletion, or COS pruning.
  • COD and COS are usable standalone (outside a CE); cleanup must not depend on any CE-side controller.
  • Handle adoption: a COS created before the COD that later manages it (same spec.group), with a matching or a new template.
  • Claim (adopt) every referenced Secret, regardless of type, so its deletion follows the COS. The object-data-only restriction is deferred to future work.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Who creates the packed Secrets, and closing the window before any COS exists. That is the creator's responsibility (CE / operator-controller), deferred. See The creator contract.
  • Changing the packing format, content-addressed naming, or immutability of the Secrets.
  • Changing how the COS validates or reports on referenced content (the existing Ready=False/PreconditionsNotMet behavior stays as-is).
  • CE-side ownership of Secrets (being removed; out of scope here).

docs.title: Anti-goals (what would make this a failure)
docs.text:
• Adopting or deleting a Secret the COS does not reference. (Deleting a Secret the COS does reference is expected — that is the GC semantics; narrowing which Secrets may be referenced is deferred to future work.)
  • A design that only avoids leaks while a CE exists (i.e. not standalone-safe).
  • Reintroducing a long-lived owner (CE or COD) that must actively remove its ownerRefs to avoid leaking — fragile bookkeeping we explicitly reject.
  • Premature deletion of a Secret a live (or just-created / just-adopted) COS still needs.

docs.title: Core principle: own, not manage
docs.text:
The object-controller (COD/COS) owns the Secrets a COS references strictly as a garbage-collection anchor — so a Secret's deletion follows the COS(es) that reference it — and does not manage them in any other sense.

  • Own = add a single, non-controller, additive, idempotent ownerRef. The COS becomes a thing whose disappearance reclaims the Secret. That one metadata write is the entire extent of what the object-controller does to a Secret.
  • Not manage = it is not the controller of the Secret; it does not watch it, does not mutate or repair its content (they are immutable; it only reads them via resolveObjectRef), and takes no responsibility for its existence or validity. A missing/invalid Secret is reported by the COS (Ready=False/PreconditionsNotMet), never created or fixed by it.

Controller=false is a direct consequence of this principle, not an incidental choice: the controller flag confers management/stewardship semantics (single controller-of-record, .Owns() watch wiring, adoption/collision arbitration) that we explicitly do not want — and that would forbid the multi-owner model (shared content referenced by several COSes). We want only the GC cascade, which works for non-controller owners.

Everything the object-controller deliberately omits — a sweeper, a finalizer, COD Secret ownership, declarative ownerRef removal — would be managing. The responsibility to manage a Secret (create it, bridge the pre-COS window, steward its content) stays with its creator (see the creator contract).

docs.title: Key facts this design relies on
docs.text:
1. Kubernetes GC deletes a dependent only when all its owners are gone. As each owner is deleted, GC strips that ownerRef; when the last referenced owner is gone, the dependent is deleted. Multiple owners therefore means "deleted when the last one goes."
  2. Manually removing an ownerRef does not delete the dependent. A dependent left with zero ownerRefs is a normal orphan and is never GC'd. Deletion only happens via owner deletion (cascade) or an explicit Delete. (This is why an owner cannot "release" a Secret by un-referencing it — it must either be deleted itself or the Secret must be explicitly deleted.)
  3. At most one Controller=true ownerRef is allowed per object. A Secret may have several non-controller owners.
  4. OwnerRefs on an immutable Secret are allowed. Immutability locks data, not metadata; main already patches ownerRefs onto immutable Secrets.
  5. Cross-scope ownerRefs are valid for a namespaced dependent owned by a cluster-scoped owner (COS/COD are cluster-scoped; Secrets are namespaced).
  6. Secret metadata is outside both identity hashes. The COD template hash is DeepHashObject(spec.template) — it covers the refs (name/namespace/key), not the Secret object. The content-addressed Secret name hashes data only. So ownerRef changes never churn a revision or rename a Secret. (Content changes do flow into identity, indirectly, via the content-addressed name in the ref.)

docs.title: The model: COS-only ownership
docs.text:
Each COS owns the Secrets its phases reference, via a non-controller ownerRef, regardless of type. That is the entire object-controller mechanism. It is sufficient because:

  • Revision churn: a new template produces a new COS that owns the new Secrets; the old COS is archived and pruned by the COD, and GC cascades its Secrets. ✔
  • COD deletion: the COD controller-owns its COSes, so deleting the COD cascades to the COSes, whose Secrets then cascade. ✔
  • Standalone COS: owns its referenced Secrets and cascades them on its own deletion — no COD required. ✔
  • Shared content: two revisions with identical content reference the same content-addressed Secret; each COS adds a non-controller ownerRef; the Secret survives until the last referencing COS is gone. ✔ (This is why ownerRefs must be non-controller.)

Everything that was ever referenced by a COS is reclaimed by COS ownership. Everything that was never referenced by a COS is, by definition, outside the object-controller's knowledge and is the creator's responsibility (below).

docs.title: What the COD does (nothing new for Secrets)
docs.text:
The COD does not own Secrets, does not run a sweeper, and needs no finalizer for Secrets. Its existing responsibilities are unchanged: it owns its COSes and prunes archived revisions, and pruning cascades Secret cleanup through COS ownership.

The COD also does not gain a PreconditionsNotMet check for referenced Secrets. A missing/invalid referenced Secret does not block COS creation; the COS reports Ready=False/PreconditionsNotMet at resolve time and recovers when the Secret appears. The COD keeps its existing validateTemplateMetadata check, which guards a different failure mode (invalid template metadata makes the COS Create itself fail at the API server). Optionally, the COD may propagate the latest revision's Ready reason/message onto its own status so a stuck precondition is legible — surfacing, not re-validating.

docs.title: Any referenced Secret is adopted and garbage-collected
docs.text:
The ref contract stays as it is today — a COS phase may reference a Secret of any type (the existing immutability precondition still applies). This design does not tighten that; see Future work.

What it adds is uniform GC semantics: every referenced Secret is adopted (owned) by the referencing COS and garbage-collected when that COS is deleted, regardless of type. The claim is not type-gated.

Known consequence: because any referenced Secret is adopted, referencing a Secret hands its lifecycle to the COS — including a user-supplied Secret a bare COS points at. That is accepted for now. The future object-data-only restriction (below) is what will eventually prevent a COS from referencing (and thus adopting) a Secret that was never meant to be OLM-managed. Until then, "referencing a Secret means the COS owns and will delete it" is the documented contract.

docs.title: Future work
docs.text:
• Restrict referenceable Secret types to object-data. Today a COS phase may reference a Secret of any type, and this design adopts+GCs whatever is referenced. A later change should make a referenced Secret that is not olm.operatorframework.io/object-data a precondition failure (Ready=False/PreconditionsNotMet), so a COS can only reference (and therefore adopt/delete) Secrets that were meant to be OLM-managed content. This removes the "referencing a user's ordinary Secret deletes it" footgun by construction. It is a tightening of the (experimental) ref contract and is deferred so this change can land the GC semantics first.
  • The CE-side creator contract (below) and the applier Controller=true → non-controller-bridge conversion.

docs.title: The creator contract (deferred, CE side)
docs.text:
A referenced Secret's lifecycle transfers to a COS once that COS adds its ownerRef. Until a COS owns it, the Secret's creator is responsible for it. A controller that uses COD/COS to manage cluster content should add a bridging ownerRef to the Secret at creation time and remove it once it observes that a COS has taken ownership.

This closes the two windows the object-controller cannot see:

  • Creation window: Secret created before any COS exists → the creator's bridge owns it, so it cascades if the creator is deleted.
  • Claim gap: a COS exists and references the Secret but has not yet patched its ownerRef → the creator holds the bridge until it confirms the COS ownerRef is present, then drops it.

Because the bridge is transient (dropped once a COS owns the Secret), it does not reintroduce the "long-lived owner never releases → leak across upgrades" problem. The t=1/t=2 orphan (template referenced a Secret at t=1, the COS was never created, template moved to t=2) is, by this contract, the creator's cleanup — its bridge cascades on creator deletion, or the creator reclaims it directly.

This contract is documented here but implemented later, on the CE / operator-controller side.

docs.title: Interaction with the existing applier ownerRef patching (main)
docs.text:
On main the operator-controller applier already owns referenced Secrets: at COS creation it patches an ownerRef with Controller=true (patchSecretOwnerReferences / ensureSecretOwnerReferences / patchOwnerRefsOnSecrets in internal/operator-controller/applier/boxcutter.go). Secret names are per-revision there (<cosName>-<hash>), so each Secret has exactly one owner and Controller=true is correct and non-conflicting today.

This PR does not modify the applier (it is CE / operator-controller side, explicitly deferred). The two mechanisms coexist cleanly:

  • For an operator-controller-created COS, the applier patches the ownerRef at creation (before the COS controller first reconciles). The COS controller's claim dedups by owner UID, sees the ref already present, and is a no-op. The flag stays Controller=true, which is fine on main (single owner per per-revision Secret).
  • For a standalone COD/COS, no applier runs, so the COS controller's claim is the sole and authoritative mechanism — adding a Controller=false ownerRef.

Consequence (intended): the non-controller / shared-content multi-owner model only fully takes effect once the deferred CE-side rework converts the applier's patching to the transient non-controller bridge (and stops setting Controller=true). Until then the headline multi-owner behavior is exercised and tested via the standalone path; the operator-controller path keeps its current main behavior unchanged. This is deliberate, and matches the "CE later" scope.

No orphan-window regression: the operator-controller path keeps at-creation applier ownership; the standalone path's pre-COS window is the creator's responsibility by contract (for a bare COS, the creator is the user).

docs.title: Adoption
docs.text:
Adoption needs no special handling because ownership rides on the COS, independent of creation order:

  • COS before COD, matching template: the COS already owns its Secrets; the COD adopts the COS as its active revision; nothing to reconcile for Secrets.
  • COS before COD, new template same group: the COD creates a new revision (which owns the new Secrets) and the pre-existing COS becomes an archived revision (still owning its Secrets until pruned, then cascaded).

There is no group-label discovery, no sweeper race, and no grace window to tune.

docs.title: What the object-controller implements
docs.text:
1. COS controller — claim referenced Secrets. For each referenced Secret in the COS's own spec phases, get the Secret and ensure a non-controller ownerRef pointing at the COS — regardless of the Secret's type. Make it idempotent and crash-recoverable (same intent as main's ensureSecretOwnerReferences): a COS that failed to patch on a prior reconcile re-attempts on the next, deduping by owner UID.
  2. Discovery is ref-driven, not label-driven. Do not reuse main's label-list discovery (List(InNamespace(SystemNamespace), MatchingLabels{RevisionNameKey: cos.Name})): a standalone COS may reference Secrets in arbitrary namespaces that carry no revision-name label, so ownership must be driven off the COS's own refs. (Builder-check Q3.)
  3. Claim on existence, independent of content validity. A referenced Secret that exists but fails a content precondition (mutable, malformed, changed) is still claimed, so it is still reclaimed when the COS is deleted. Wire the claim so it is not gated behind the content short-circuits — ownership tracks lifecycle, not content health; the preconditions are reported separately. (Builder-check Q4.)
  4. No type gate. This design does not restrict which Secret types may be referenced (see Future work), so the claim owns every referenced Secret.
  5. COS controller — precondition reporting unchanged. Keep the existing Ready=False/PreconditionsNotMet behavior for missing / mutable / changed / malformed referenced content.
  6. COD controller — no Secret logic. Confirm pruning an archived COS cascades its Secrets (it does, via COS ownership). Keep validateTemplateMetadata. Optionally propagate the latest revision's Ready reason/message onto the COD condition.
  7. RBAC. The object-controller needs Secret get/list/update in the namespaces it resolves refs from. It does not need Secret delete (cascade handles deletion).
  8. Docs. Record the creator contract where COD/COS behavior is documented.

docs.title: Testing approach
docs.text:
• Unit (COS claim): ensures a non-controller ownerRef is added to each referenced Secret regardless of type; is idempotent; additive-only + UID-dedup (no-op when an ownerRef with the COS's UID already exists); re-adds after a simulated prior failure; claims on existence independent of content validity; skips a not-yet-created Secret; claims a referenced Secret once even when multiple objects reference it.
  • Unit (COD): pruning an archived revision does not require any Secret-level action; validateTemplateMetadata unchanged.
  • envtest (ownerRef write, not cascade): envtest runs only kube-apiserver
  • etcd — not kube-controller-manager — so the garbage collector does not run there and cascade deletion cannot be asserted in envtest. Use envtest only to validate the write against a real API server:
  • The claim patch is accepted on an immutable Secret (confirms metadata is patchable despite immutability) and is idempotent across a real Get/Patch roundtrip.
  • Coexistence: a Secret already carrying an applier-style Controller=true ownerRef is not double-ref'd by the claim (UID-dedup no-op).
  • GC cascade is an e2e concern (see below) because only a real cluster runs the garbage collector.

Adoption needs no dedicated secret test: with COS-only ownership and no sweeper, nothing deletes Secrets except k8s GC on owner deletion, so there is no premature-deletion path for adoption to trigger. Ownership simply rides on the COS.

docs.title: E2E (standalone COD/COS)
docs.text:
These are the end-to-end, user-observable scenarios for this PR. They live in the experimental suites (@BoxcutterRuntime) alongside the existing revision.feature / cos_*.feature / cod_*.feature, which already create and reference object-data Secrets. They exercise the standalone path — a COD/COS driven directly, with no ClusterExtension/applier involved — which is where this PR's new behavior is actually observable (the operator-controller path is unchanged; see "Interaction with the existing applier").

  1. Standalone COS cleanup. Create an object-data Secret and a COS that references it; the COS becomes Ready. Confirm the Secret carries a (non-controller) ownerRef to the COS. Delete the COS → the referenced object-data Secret is eventually removed (cascade).
  2. Standalone COD cleanup. Create a COD whose template references object-data Secret content; it rolls out a revision (COS). Delete the COD → its COS revision(s) and their object-data Secrets are eventually removed.
  3. Type-agnostic adoption + GC. Create a COS that references an immutable, non-object-data (e.g. Opaque) Secret holding a manifest; the COS becomes Ready and the Secret gains a non-controller ownerRef to the COS. Delete the COS → the Secret is eventually removed. This pins the "any referenced Secret is adopted and garbage-collected" contract (and documents that referencing a Secret hands its lifecycle to the COS, pending the future type restriction).

Regression guard (existing, not new). uninstall.feature's "Removing ClusterExtension cascades to grouped revisions and their content Secrets" covers the CE → COS → Secret cascade. This PR is additive (applier untouched), so that scenario must continue to pass; name it as a guard rather than modifying it.

Step reuse: the suites already have steps for applying a COS/COD, waiting on Ready, creating object-data Secrets, and asserting a resource "is installed" / "is eventually not found". Scenarios 1–3 should compose from those plus (if not present) a step asserting a Secret's ownerRef points at a given COS and a step asserting a Secret still exists after a deletion.

docs.title: What's left to the builder
docs.text:
• The precise call site in the COS controller for the claim step, and whether to reuse/relocate the existing main ownerRef helpers (patchOwnerRefsOnSecrets, ensureSecretOwnerReferences) from the CE-side applier into an object-controller-owned helper. (Today those live in internal/operator-controller/applier/boxcutter.go and set Controller=true; the object-controller version must set Controller=false.)
  • Whether to resolve a ref's default namespace (empty → OLM system namespace) before claiming, matching how resolveObjectRef resolves it.
  • Whether, and exactly how, to propagate the latest revision's Ready reason/message onto the COD condition (the optional legibility improvement).
  • Exact RBAC marker changes and manifest regeneration.

docs.title: Design: ClusterObjectDeployment adoption of existing ClusterObjectSets
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-26 Status: Draft (pending approval) Branch: cod-adopt-existing-cos (off upstream/main @ 5e8f2748)

docs.title: Intent and why
docs.text:
A ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) manages a family of ClusterObjectSet (COS) revisions, identified by spec.group == COD.name. Today the COD controller only creates revisions it owns; it does not take ownership of COSes in its group that it did not create.
