This design makes the COD adopt the ClusterObjectSets in its group so it owns the exact revision family boxcutter already treats as siblings.

Driving scenario — Helm→COD migration. To migrate a Helm-based install to COD/COS management, the migrator creates an initial orphaned COS (revision 1) with collisionProtection: None directly. None lets that first revision adopt the objects the Helm applier already created on the cluster (they are otherwise "foreign" and would collide). Creating that COS explicitly guarantees the None-initial-revision exists; relying on the COD to mint revision 1 from its template would expose a race where a subsequent reconcile mutates the template's collisionProtection around revision-1 creation, so the clean adopting revision might not be produced. So: the migrator deterministically creates the orphan revision 1, and the COD adopts it.

Once revision 1 (None) owns the Helm objects, they are inside the revision family, so the COD rolling revision 2 from its template (collisionProtection: Prevent) hands those objects over from the sibling revision 1 — no collision, because Prevent only blocks foreign objects, not sibling-owned ones. So adoption followed by normal rollout is correct by construction; no re-rollout suppression is needed.

Secondary scenario (narrow — see caveat): a COD deleted while its COSes survive (orphaned with no controller owner), then recreated, re-adopts them. Caveat: this only holds when the surviving COSes are genuinely owner-less. If a COD is deleted with its COSes left intact (no cascade), those COSes still carry a controller ownerRef to the old COD's UID; a recreated same-named COD has a new UID, so SetControllerReference returns AlreadyOwnedError and the COD reports RevisionOwnershipConflict rather than re-adopting (we honor fail-on-different- controller). True re-adoption across a delete/recreate with surviving owned COSes is out of scope — in practice Kubernetes cascade deletion removes the COSes with the COD, so the owner-less window is what the migrator (which creates owner-less orphans) actually exercises.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• The COD controller-owns every COS in its group (spec.group == COD.name) — the exact set boxcutter treats as the sibling family.
  • Adopt orphans (COSes with no controller owner); fail on a COS owned by a different controller (anomaly — see below); no-op on COSes it already owns.
  • Revision numbering accounts for adopted revisions: the next revision is max(revision over all group COSes) + 1 (or 1 if none), so a freshly created revision never collides with an adopted one.
  • Ownership uses the native controller reference — the same mechanism the COS's boxcutter configuration (ownerhandling.NewNative) uses for objects.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• The migrator creating the orphan collisionProtection: None revision 1 (operator-controller / CE side). This branch is the COD's adoption behavior only.
  • Secret ownership / GC, and any ClusterExtension-side changes.
  • Re-rollout suppression or template-hash stamping onto adopted revisions (not needed — see rollout mechanics above).

docs.title: Anti-goals (what would make this a failure)
docs.text:
• Stealing a COS that is controller-owned by a different controller (we fail loudly instead).
  • Minting a new revision whose number/name collides with an adopted revision.
  • Suppressing or special-casing rollout after adoption (the sibling hand-off makes the normal path correct).

docs.title: How boxcutter defines "siblings" (grounding)
docs.text:
Boxcutter does not discover siblings itself — the COS controller tells it. In buildClusterObjectSet/buildBoxcutterPhases the COS: 1. lists COSes sharing spec.group via the group field index (clusterObjectSetGroupIndex), active and non-deleting, excluding itself; and 2. passes them to boxcutter as boxcutter.WithSiblingOwners(siblingObjs).

Boxcutter then treats an object controlled by the current revision or a sibling owner as legitimate (adopt / hand off), and an object controlled by a non-sibling foreign controller as a collision (gated by collisionProtection).

So the sibling family is defined by spec.group. Because spec.group == COD.name, only one COD can ever own a given group — which is why a foreign-controlled COS in a COD's group is an anomaly, not a legitimate sibling, and adoption fails on it.

docs.title: Ownership reconciliation (ensureRevisionOwnership)
docs.text:
On every COD reconcile, before rollout and garbage collection, the COD ensures it controller-owns every COS in its group:

  1. List COSes with spec.group == COD.name (the same group index the COS uses for siblings; include active and archived — the COD owns its whole history).
  2. For each such COS, call controllerutil.SetControllerReference(cod, cos, scheme):
  3. no controller owner → the ref is set; Update the COS (adopt).
  4. already owned by this COD (same UID) → no change; skip the Update.
  5. owned by a different controller → SetControllerReference returns *controllerutil.AlreadyOwnedError. The COD does not steal it and does not silently tolerate it: set Progressing=False with reason RevisionOwnershipConflict on the COD (message naming the conflicting COS and its controller), skip rollout for this reconcile, persist status, and requeue so the anomaly is both visible on the COD and retried. (A bare reconcile error would only surface in logs; the condition is the actionable signal.)
  6. Only issue an Update when the ownerReferences actually changed (avoid write churn / needless reconciles).

A new condition reason is added to the API: ClusterObjectDeploymentReasonRevisionOwnershipConflict = "RevisionOwnershipConflict" (alongside the existing Progressing reasons in clusterobjectdeployment_types.go).

This runs before createRevision, so the COD never tries to create a revision whose name/number collides with an unowned orphan it should have adopted first.

docs.title: Revision numbering
docs.text: nextRevisionNumber returns max(.spec.revision over all COSes in the group) + 1, or 1 when the group is empty. Counting all group revisions (adopted, created, active, archived) guarantees a new revision never reuses an adopted number: after adopting ext-1, the COD mints ext-2. This resolves the existing TODO: revisit AlreadyExists handling under the adoption use-case.

docs.title: Rollout (unchanged, correct by construction)
docs.text: After adoption the adopted revision is an ordinary COD-owned revision. Normal rollout proceeds: if the template differs from the latest revision's template hash, the COD cuts the next revision; its objects are handed over from the adopted sibling revision. No special-casing.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text:
• Multiple orphans in the group: adopt all of them (each via SetControllerReference + Update).
  • Foreign-controlled COS in the group: the COD reports Progressing=False / RevisionOwnershipConflict (message naming the COS and its controller), skips rollout, and requeues until the anomaly is resolved — intentional, since group membership is exclusive to one COD.
  • Archived orphan revisions: adopted too (ownership spans the full history so GC/retention and cascade-on-COD-deletion manage them).
  • Adopted revision lacks a template-hash label: fine — the COD rolls the next revision per normal template comparison; the adopted revision is retained/pruned as history.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Unit (COD controller):
  • adopts an orphan COS in the group (controllerRef set to the COD);
  • no-op when the COS is already COD-owned (no spurious Update);
  • when a group COS is owned by a different controller, the COD reports Progressing=False / RevisionOwnershipConflict and does not roll out (rather than silently proceeding or only logging);
  • adopts multiple orphans;
  • includes archived revisions;
  • ignores COSes outside the group (spec.group != COD.name).
  • nextRevisionNumber = max over all group revisions + 1 (and 1 when empty); a freshly created revision after adopting ext-1 is ext-2.
  • envtest: adoption Update is accepted against a real API server; a COS controller-owned by a different controller yields AlreadyOwnedError and is not modified.
  • e2e: a COD created over an orphan COS in its group ends up owning it (COD is the controller owner), and a subsequent template change rolls the next revision that supersedes it. (Migration-driven e2e belongs with the migrator work.)

docs.title: What's left to the builder
docs.text:
• The exact placement of ensureRevisionOwnership in the reconcile sequence (before garbageCollectArchivedRevisions and reconcileRollout) and whether to reuse the existing group-list helper.
  • Whether to detect "already owned / needs no update" by comparing ownerReferences before vs after SetControllerReference (to gate the Update), or via metav1.GetControllerOf.
  • Error-type matching for AlreadyOwnedError (errors.As) and the exact reconcile error wrapping/condition surfaced.

docs.title: ClusterObjectDeployment Progressing reasons: surfacing why a rollout is impeded
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-27 Status: Design — approved for planning Branch: cod-progressing-reasons

docs.title: Intent and why
docs.text:
The ClusterObjectDeployment (COD) Progressing condition today collapses every in-flight rollout into a single reason: whenever the head active ClusterObjectSet (COS) revision has not completed, the COD reports Progressing=True / NewClusterObjectSetProgressing with a generic message. The only non-progressing outcomes are NewClusterObjectSetProgressed (done), ProgressDeadlineExceeded, and InvalidSpecification (the COD's own template metadata is invalid).

This is opaque to a COD user. When a rollout is stuck, the user's real question is "is this rollout impeded in a way that requires me to act, and what do I do?" — not merely "is it done yet?". The head active COS already knows the answer via its own Ready condition reason (Pending, ObjectsNotReady, PreconditionsNotMet, ObjectCollision, InvalidSpecification, AllObjectsReady, Superseded, Archiving, Archived). The COD flattens all of that away.

This change gives the COD Progressing condition a small, COD-level vocabulary that classifies the head active COS's Ready state into "rollout proceeding normally" versus "rollout impeded, needs intervention," and carries the remedy in the message.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Distinguish, on the COD Progressing condition, a normally-progressing rollout from one that is impeded and needs user intervention.
  • For each impeded cause, surface a distinct, stable, machine-matchable reason and a human-readable message describing what to do.
  • Follow Kubernetes condition conventions: Progressing=False means the rollout is stalled and will not advance without intervention; Progressing=True means it is progressing or is expected to (still retrying).
  • Keep the user-facing documentation in lockstep: the conditions field docstring (the CRD schema description), the regenerated api-reference, and the concept docs must all describe the new reasons.
  • Cover the new behavior with e2e tests, not just unit tests.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• No change to the COD Available condition or its reasons.
  • No change to the COS Ready condition, its reasons, or the COS controller.
  • No 1:1 mirroring of COS reason strings onto the COD. The COD uses its own deployment-altitude vocabulary ("revision" = the head active COS).
  • No change to how or when revisions are created, archived, or garbage collected.
  • No change to the progress-deadline mechanism itself (only its precedence relative to the new hard-stall reasons).

docs.title: Anti-goals (what would make this a failure even if it technically works)
docs.text:
• A user still cannot tell a "just wait" rollout from a "go fix something" rollout at a glance.
  • Reasons that churn on every reconcile (reason/message flapping) or that are too fine-grained to match in automation.
  • Conflating the COD's own invalid template metadata with an invalid head revision — a user must be able to tell which spec is wrong.

docs.title: Decisions made (by the human partner)
docs.text:
1. COD-level vocabulary, not a faithful 1:1 re-export of the COS Ready reason string.
  2. Progressing True/False per cause follows Kubernetes convention:
  3. InvalidSpecification (head COS) → Progressing=False (hard stall)
  4. ObjectCollision (head COS) → Progressing=False (hard stall)
  5. PreconditionsNotMet (head COS) → Progressing=True (keeps retrying)
  6. Pending / ObjectsNotReady (head COS) → Progressing=True (normal)
  7. Hard stalls short-circuit the deadline. If the head revision is already stalled on an actionable cause (ObjectCollision / InvalidSpecification), report that — it is more useful than ProgressDeadlineExceeded. The deadline governs only the still-retrying states (PreconditionsNotMet, ObjectsNotReady, Pending).
  8. Use generic, COD-owned messages that name the head revision — do not echo the COS Ready message. Each mapped reason gets a concise, stable COD-owned message that identifies the head ClusterObjectSet and points the user to inspect it for specifics (the Deployment→Pod inspection pattern: a Deployment does not echo its Pod's message). This keeps the COD condition message COD-owned and decoupled from COS message formatting; the authoritative, always-current detail lives on the revision. Reusing the COS message verbatim is a trivial future upgrade if inline remedies are later wanted.

docs.title: Note on PreconditionsNotMet (the accepted coarseness)
docs.text:
PreconditionsNotMet is not probe/assertion failure — probe failures live under ObjectsNotReady. But grounding the design against the COS controller showed PreconditionsNotMet is coarser than first assumed: the COS emits it, and always retries it on a flat timer, for a mix of genuinely recoverable causes (mutable referenced Secret, RBAC not yet granted, dependency CRD not yet propagated) and permanent spec errors that only a spec change can fix (the same object in two phases, a manifest carrying ownerReferences) — because the boxcutter dry-run cannot tell them apart (clusterobjectset_controller.go:162,178,206,257,280; cos_static_validation.feature).

Decision: the COD keeps the simple mapping and defers to the COS's own classification — PreconditionsNotMet → Progressing=True / RevisionPreconditionsNotMet, with a generic COD-owned message naming the revision (decision 4) that directs the user to inspect the revision for the specific cause. Permanent cases that masquerade as PreconditionsNotMet therefore show as "progressing/retrying" until they eventually trip ProgressDeadlineExceeded; the COD does not try to out-guess the COS. Making this distinction crisp would require teaching the COS/boxcutter layer to separate permanent from transient preflight rejections — explicitly out of scope here, a possible follow-up.

docs.title: Note on InvalidSpecification reachability
docs.text: ClusterObjectSetReasonInvalidSpecification is emitted at a single site (clusterobjectset_controller.go:186, for a configValidationError), and CRD admission validation blocks nearly every construction path, so a COD template that passes admission can realistically reach it only via an edge case (e.g. a malformed progression-probe label selector). The RevisionInvalidSpecification reason and mapping are still implemented for completeness, but it is covered by a unit test only — not a deterministic e2e. The hard-stall-beats-deadline precedence is locked via ObjectCollision, which is reliably reachable.

docs.title: Proposed reason set
docs.text:
The head active COS is framed as "the revision" — the COD's natural altitude.

Head active COS Ready reason COD Progressing COD reason COD message Pending, ObjectsNotReady True NewClusterObjectSetProgressing (existing) existing generic "latest revision is progressing" PreconditionsNotMet True RevisionPreconditionsNotMet (new) generic, names the revision, points to inspect it ObjectCollision False RevisionObjectCollision (new) generic, names the revision, points to inspect it InvalidSpecification False RevisionInvalidSpecification (new) generic, names the revision, points to inspect it AllObjectsReady n/a handled via CompletedAt → NewClusterObjectSetProgressed (existing) rollout complete

For the three mapped reasons the COD message is a concise COD-owned sentence that names the head ClusterObjectSet and directs the user to inspect it (decision 4); exact phrasing is the builder's call, following the repo's condition-message style. The default/progressing path keeps its existing bespoke wording.

Unchanged existing reasons that remain:

  • NewClusterObjectSetProgressed — head revision completed (CompletedAt set).
  • ProgressDeadlineExceeded — a still-retrying rollout exceeded its deadline.
  • InvalidSpecification — the COD's own template metadata is invalid (set before a revision is even created). Deliberately kept distinct from RevisionInvalidSpecification so the user can tell which spec is wrong.

Reasons stay a small, stable, machine-matchable set. The specific "what to do" (including, where useful, the head COS's own Ready message) lives in the COD Progressing message, not in the reason string.

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text:
reconcileRollout in internal/object-controller/controllers/clusterobjectdeployment_controller.go sets Progressing through setProgressing(cod, status, reason, message). The revised ordering (hard stalls short-circuit the deadline; the deadline governs only still-retrying states):

  1. COD template metadata invalid → Progressing=False / InvalidSpecification (existing, unchanged — runs before a revision exists).
  2. Ensure the desired revision exists (create if template changed / none). On create error → Progressing=True / NewClusterObjectSetProgressing (existing, unchanged).
  3. Head revision completed (CompletedAt set) → Progressing=False / NewClusterObjectSetProgressed (existing, unchanged).
  4. (new) Read the head revision's Ready condition reason:
  5. InvalidSpecification → Progressing=False / RevisionInvalidSpecification
  6. ObjectCollision → Progressing=False / RevisionObjectCollision

These short-circuit the deadline. 5. Deadline exceeded → Progressing=False / ProgressDeadlineExceeded (existing — now reached only for still-retrying states). 6. (new) Head revision Ready reason is PreconditionsNotMet → Progressing=True / RevisionPreconditionsNotMet. 7. Otherwise (Pending, ObjectsNotReady, missing/empty Ready condition, or any unrecognized reason) → Progressing=True / NewClusterObjectSetProgressing (existing default).

The head revision's Ready condition is read with apimeta.FindStatusCondition(latest.Status.Conditions, ocv1.ClusterObjectSetTypeReady). A missing or non-matching reason falls through to the default progressing branch (step 7), so partially-populated or future COS reasons never produce a false hard stall.

docs.title: Builder's remaining latitude
docs.text:
• Message phrasing. The COD message is a generic, COD-owned sentence that names the head ClusterObjectSet and directs the user to inspect it (decision 4) — it must not echo the COS Ready message. Exact wording is the builder's call, following the repo's condition-message style. The reason strings and True/False mapping are fixed above.
  • Reconcile result / requeue for the new branches. Match the existing behavior of the branch each new case sits near (hard-stall False branches return without a bespoke timed requeue and rely on the COS watch, as the completed/invalid branches do today; PreconditionsNotMet sits with the still-retrying states and keeps whatever requeue the deadline path already computes). Note the controller's deadlineAwareRateLimiter may still inject a deadline-based requeue on an active head revision even when a branch returns a zero ctrl.Result{}; this is harmless (idempotent re-report) since the COD also Watches owned COSes.
  • Test structure. Extend the existing tabular tests in clusterobjectdeployment_controller_test.go and clusterobjectdeployment_deadline_test.go rather than adding standalone tests (per the per-PR consistency preference). Cover: each new reason; the hard-stall-beats-deadline precedence via ObjectCollision; PreconditionsNotMet staying True under the deadline and flipping to ProgressDeadlineExceeded past it; and the unrecognized/missing-reason fallthrough. Also flip the existing invalid specification subtest in clusterobjectdeployment_deadline_test.go (currently asserts ProgressDeadlineExceeded for a past-deadline COS with Ready=False/InvalidSpecification): under the new precedence it must now assert RevisionInvalidSpecification.

docs.title: Documentation to update
docs.text:
These are required parts of the change, not optional follow-ups.

  • conditions field docstring in api/v1/clusterobjectdeployment_types.go (ClusterObjectDeploymentStatus.Conditions, currently lines ~142–157). It enumerates the Progressing reasons prose-style; extend it to describe RevisionPreconditionsNotMet (True), RevisionObjectCollision (False), RevisionInvalidSpecification (False), and that these reflect the head active revision's own Ready state. Keep the existing distinction between the COD's own InvalidSpecification (template metadata) and the revision's RevisionInvalidSpecification. This docstring is the CRD schema field description, so it must be regenerated (see Constraints).
  • Regenerated artifacts: run make manifests crd-ref-docs so the standard and experimental CRD YAMLs and docs/api-reference/olmv1-api-reference.md pick up the revised description. Commit the regenerated files.
  • Concept docs: review docs/draft/concepts/clusterobjectsets.md (and any COD-facing concept/how-to page) for a place that explains COD rollout status / Progressing reasons, and add the new impeded-rollout reasons with their "what to do" guidance. If no such section exists, add a short one — the whole point of this change is user-facing discoverability.

docs.title: e2e coverage (required)
docs.text:
Add e2e coverage for the new reasons, following the existing COD feature-file patterns (test/e2e/features/cod_rollout.feature, cod_progression_timeout.feature, cod_template_metadata.feature). The builder may extend an existing feature or add a new cod_progressing_reasons.feature; whichever reads more consistently with the suite.

Scenarios to cover, each asserting the COD Progressing condition's status + reason:

  • RevisionObjectCollision (False): pre-create an object that the head revision's phase will collide with (owned by another controller / already existing), roll out a COD whose template produces that object, assert Progressing=False / RevisionObjectCollision. (See the collision/adoption facts already established for COS e2e — two independent bare owners collide.)
  • RevisionInvalidSpecification (False): unit test only — this COS state is not reliably reachable from an admission-passing COD template (see the reachability note above), so do not add a deterministic e2e for it.
  • RevisionPreconditionsNotMet (True): drive the head revision into PreconditionsNotMet (e.g. a referenced-content precondition that is not yet satisfied, mirroring the COS revision.feature referenced-content scenario), assert Progressing=True / RevisionPreconditionsNotMet, and ideally that it recovers to progressing/complete once the precondition is satisfied.
  • Hard-stall-beats-deadline precedence: an ObjectCollision stall reports RevisionObjectCollision rather than ProgressDeadlineExceeded even after the deadline would have elapsed. (A unit test must lock this too, and is the authoritative check; the e2e is belt-and-suspenders. ObjectCollision is used here because InvalidSpecification is not reliably reachable in e2e.)

Run the standard e2e as experimental-gated per the COD e2e workflow in AGENTS.md and the e2e local validation notes. If any of these states is impractical to reach deterministically in e2e, note it in the PR and rely on the unit test for that case rather than a flaky scenario.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The reason constants themselves are plain string consts in api/v1/clusterobjectdeployment_types.go and are not part of the CRD schema. However, the conditions field docstring that enumerates the reasons is the CRD schema field description, and this change updates it — so make manifests crd-ref-docs is required, and the regenerated CRD YAMLs and docs/api-reference/olmv1-api-reference.md must be committed. No DeepCopy change is expected (no new Go fields). Run make lint and make test-unit before opening the PR, and make verify to confirm generated artifacts are in sync.
  • Experimental API surface (COD lives behind the experimental feature gate), so no compatibility guarantee is owed on these reason strings — but they should still be chosen to last.
  • This is COD-controller-side only. No COS controller, migrator, or CRD changes.

docs.title: Design: Decouple object-controller Helm rendering from featureSet/Boxcutter
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-04 Size: small change

docs.title: Intent / Why
docs.text:
Today helm template fails when object-controller would be rendered in the standard profile. The failure comes from the objectController.enabled helper in helm/olmv1/templates/_helpers.tpl, which conflates two unrelated concerns:

  1. Generation — whether object-controller manifests are emitted.
  2. Runtime — whether operator-controller uses object-controller (the BoxcutterRuntime feature gate).

Because of this conflation, enabling BoxcutterRuntime implicitly turns on object-controller generation, and a non-experimental featureSet then triggers fail "objectController requires options.featureSet=experimental", aborting the whole render instead of simply producing no object-controller manifests.

We want: standard renders nothing for object-controller (no error), experimental renders it, and BoxcutterRuntime is only a runtime flag.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Standard profile renders no object-controller resources, with no error.
  • Experimental profile renders object-controller resources as today.
  • BoxcutterRuntime becomes purely a --feature-gates arg on operator-controller; it no longer drives object-controller generation.
  • object-controller remains an independent, explicit toggle (standalone deploy).
  • The shared/common resources (namespace, default deny-all NetworkPolicy) render iff at least one component is enabled — never orphaned, never missing.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• No change to featureSet semantics (CRD schema selection + feature-set label).
  • No new values files (standard = chart defaults, experimental = overlay).
  • No change to operator-controller / catalogd gating.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• object-controller CRDs only exist under base/object-controller/crd/experimental/ and the CRD templates hardcode that path (no featureSet branch), so enabled: true renders the experimental CRDs regardless of featureSet. .Files.Get returns empty for missing files, so no render error is possible.
  • Shell/Helm behavior must stay cross-platform (no new tooling).

docs.title: Approaches considered
docs.text:
• A. Key generation off featureSet == experimental. Zero new config, but keeps object-controller welded to the profile and removes the independent toggle.
  • B. Explicit objectController.enabled knob, defaulted per overlay (chosen). enabled: false default, enabled: true in the experimental overlay. Keeps a standalone toggle and cleanly separates generation from the Boxcutter runtime flag.
  • Rejected a dedicated commonResources.enabled variable for the shared resources in favour of gating them on "at least one component enabled" — same outcome with no new surface area.

docs.title: 1. objectController.enabled helper (helm/olmv1/templates/_helpers.tpl)
docs.text:
Simplify to a plain boolean gate:

  • Remove the null -> $boxcutterEnabled default.
  • Remove the $boxcutterEnabled && enabled==false -> fail guard.
  • Remove the featureSet != experimental -> fail guard.
  • Also drop the now-dead BoxcutterRuntime both-lists conflict fail from this helper (it is about runtime gate config, not object-controller generation).

Result: returns true when options.objectController.enabled is true, empty otherwise.

docs.title: 2. Values
docs.text:
• helm/olmv1/values.yaml: set options.objectController.enabled: false (replacing the null default and its Boxcutter-follows comment).
  • helm/experimental.yaml: add options.objectController.enabled: true.

docs.title: 3. Common resources gate
docs.text:
Guard both helm/olmv1/templates/namespace.yml and helm/olmv1/templates/networkpolicy/networkpolicy-olmv1-system-default-deny-all-traffic.yml with three plain boolean reads (symmetric; the helper is now a dumb passthrough):

{{- if or .Values.options.catalogd.enabled .Values.options.operatorController.enabled .Values.options.objectController.enabled -}}
...
{{- end -}}

So they render whenever any component is on, and are omitted when nothing is enabled (e.g. a standalone object-controller render with enabled: false).

docs.title: Net effect
docs.text:
• make manifests -> standard.yaml: no object-controller resources, no error.
  • make manifests -> experimental.yaml: object-controller rendered (overlay).
  • Namespace + deny-all render iff >=1 component enabled.
  • BoxcutterRuntime only toggles --feature-gates=BoxcutterRuntime=true/false.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• make manifests succeeds; diff manifests/standard.yaml (object-controller gone) and manifests/experimental.yaml (unchanged content for object-controller).
  • helm template olmv1 helm/olmv1 (standard) succeeds with no object-controller docs.
  • helm template olmv1 helm/olmv1 --values helm/experimental.yaml renders them.
  • Standalone: operator-controller + catalogd disabled, objectController.enabled=false -> no namespace / deny-all emitted.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• Exact comment wording in values.yaml.
  • Whether make manifests surfaces any unrelated regenerated diffs to commit.

docs.title: ClusterObjectSet Ready condition
docs.text:
This document describes the single Ready status condition published on ClusterObjectSet (COS), every reason it can carry, what triggers each reason, and how the controller re-enqueues the object afterwards.

It reflects the implementation in internal/object-controller/controllers/clusterobjectset_controller.go.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A ClusterObjectSet is an immutable snapshot of Kubernetes objects. The controller rolls those objects out phase-by-phase and reports the result on a single Ready condition (type Ready). Rollout completion is recorded separately on status.completedAt; Ready reports health, not progress.

status:
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True" | "False"        # Unknown before the first reconcile
      reason: <see table below>
      message: <human-readable detail>
      observedGeneration: <generation the condition was computed for>
  • status: Unknown is the implicit initial state — before the first reconciliation has evaluated the object set there is no Ready condition at all.
  • status: True means every object is ready and passes its probes.
  • status: False means the object set is not (yet) healthy, or cannot progress. The reason distinguishes a transient hiccup from a state that needs the user to act.

docs.title: How re-enqueue works
docs.text:
The controller's re-enqueue behavior is determined entirely by what reconcile returns to controller-runtime:

Return Effect return ctrl.Result{}, err (non-nil error) Rate-limited requeue — controller-runtime re-enqueues with exponential backoff (default workqueue rate limiter). The error is also logged. return ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: N}, nil Timed requeue — re-enqueued after exactly N. return ctrl.Result{}, nil No scheduled requeue — the object is only reconciled again when a watched object changes (the tracking cache watches the objects the COS manages) or on the informer resync.

Two terms used below:

  • Retryable — the controller expects the situation to clear on its own and arranges (or relies on) another reconcile. No user action is strictly required.
  • Blocking — the situation will not clear without a change the controller cannot make itself (fix a referenced resource, or create a new object set). The controller does not keep retrying on a timer; it re-evaluates on the next reconcile trigger (spec change, watched-object change, or resync).

docs.title: The progress deadline overlay
docs.text:
spec.progressDeadlineMinutes sets a deadline for the object set to become ready. When the deadline is exceeded, most not-ready reasons are relabelled to ProgressDeadlineExceeded by setReadyWithDeadline, with the message:

The object set did not become ready within <N> minute(s). Last status: <original message>

ProgressDeadlineExceeded is an overlay, not a terminal state: the deadline does not stop reconciliation. If the objects later become ready, the next reconcile flips Ready back to True/AllObjectsReady. The re-enqueue behavior of a deadline-exceeded reconcile is inherited from the underlying path (see the "under deadline" column below).

Precedence. Two reasons are checked before the deadline and therefore take precedence over it — they are never relabelled to ProgressDeadlineExceeded:

  1. MutableReferencedSecret
  2. ResolvedContentChanged

Both are more actionable than "deadline exceeded", so they win.

docs.title: AllObjectsReady
docs.text:
• Status: True
  • Class: Terminal (success)
  • Trigger: The revision reconcile is complete (rres.IsComplete()) and every object passes its progress probe. On the first success the controller also stamps status.completedAt.
  • Message: All objects are ready and pass their probes.
  • Re-enqueue: None (Result{}). The object is reconciled again only when a watched object changes, so a later health regression is still caught.
  • Under deadline: n/a — the deadline overlay only applies to not-ready states.

docs.title: ObjectsNotReady
docs.text:
• Status: False
  • Class: Retryable (health)
  • Trigger: Rollout is not complete — one or more objects have not yet passed their progress probe.
  • Message: <N> object(s) are not yet ready. (count only; per-object detail is logged at V(1)), or the generic Objects are not yet ready. before any probe reports.
  • Re-enqueue: If spec.progressDeadlineMinutes is set, RequeueAfter: <time remaining until the deadline>. Otherwise none (Result{}) — recovery is driven by the tracking-cache watches on the managed objects (a probe flipping to ready re-triggers the reconcile).
  • Under deadline: Relabelled to ProgressDeadlineExceeded, the message collapses to the generic Objects are not yet ready., and the reconcile returns Result{} (no timer — watch-driven from here).

docs.title: Superseded
docs.text:
• Status: False
  • Class: Retryable (health)
  • Trigger: One or more objects have been adopted by a newer sibling revision (machinery.ActionProgressed). boxcutter emits ActionProgressed only for a newer sibling (a foreign owner is an ObjectCollision), so no revision comparison is needed. A partial hand-off counts; evaluated before ObjectsNotReady.
  • Message: Object(s) have been adopted by a newer revision of the object set.
  • Re-enqueue: If spec.progressDeadlineMinutes is set, RequeueAfter: <time remaining until the deadline>; otherwise none (Result{}).
  • Under deadline: Not reached — the deadline is checked first, so an exceeded deadline reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded instead.

docs.title: ValidationFailed
docs.text:
• Status: False
  • Class: Retryable
  • Trigger: Revision- or phase-level preflight validation failed (rres.GetValidationError() or pres.GetValidationError()).
  • Message: Object set manifests are invalid: <err> (revision level) or Phase <i> is invalid: <err> (phase level).
  • Re-enqueue: RequeueAfter: 10s.
  • Under deadline: Relabelled to ProgressDeadlineExceeded; still RequeueAfter: 10s.

docs.title: ObjectCollision
docs.text:
• Status: False
  • Class: Retryable
  • Trigger: An object the COS would apply already exists and is not managed by this object set — owned by another controller/operator, or a pre-existing unowned object — and CollisionProtection prevents adoption.
  • Message: One or more objects in phase <i> already exist and are not managed by this object set. (The full list of colliding objects is written to the controller log.)
  • Re-enqueue: RequeueAfter: 10s.
  • Under deadline: Relabelled to ProgressDeadlineExceeded; still RequeueAfter: 10s.

docs.title: MutableReferencedSecret
docs.text:
• Status: False
  • Class: Blocking
  • Trigger: A referenced Secret is not immutable (verifyReferencedSecretsImmutable fails). This check runs first, so it blocks before anything else is evaluated.
  • Message: Lists the offending Secrets (sorted) and explains that they must set immutable: true (or that immutable Secrets should be referenced instead).
  • Re-enqueue: None (Result{}, nil error). The controller does not retry on a timer; it re-evaluates on the next reconcile trigger (e.g. a spec change or a change to the referenced Secret).
  • Under deadline: Not overridden — because it is checked before the deadline logic, it always wins over ProgressDeadlineExceeded.

docs.title: ResolvedContentChanged
docs.text:
• Status: False
  • Class: Blocking (effectively terminal)
  • Trigger: Current phase content digests differ from those recorded in status.observedPhases (verifyObservedPhases fails) — a referenced object source was changed, or deleted and recreated with different content.
  • Message: Names the affected phase(s) and explains that the resolved content no longer matches the digest recorded in status.observedPhases, instructing the user to create a new object set to apply the changes.
  • Re-enqueue: None (Result{}, nil error). A COS snapshot is immutable, so this does not self-heal — the user must create a new object set.
  • Under deadline: Not overridden — checked before the deadline logic, so it always wins over ProgressDeadlineExceeded.

docs.title: Transient errors (no reason)
docs.text: A transient internal error — building the boxcutter phases, creating the revision engine, freeing informers, establishing the watch, the revision reconcile itself, reading a referenced Secret, listing sibling revisions, or an archive teardown error — does not write the Ready condition. The reconcile returns a non-nil error, so controller-runtime re-enqueues with rate-limited exponential backoff, and Ready keeps whatever value it had (absent on a first reconcile, read as Unknown). There is no dedicated transient-error reason.

docs.title: Archiving
docs.text:
• Status: False
  • Class: Retryable
  • Trigger: Archive teardown is in progress but not yet complete (tdres != nil && !tdres.IsComplete()), reached via spec.lifecycleState: Archived. A teardown error is a transient error and leaves Ready unchanged (see "Transient errors"), not Archiving.
  • Message: The object set is being archived; removing owned objects.
  • Re-enqueue: RequeueAfter: 5s.
  • Under deadline: n/a — the archive path has no deadline overlay.

docs.title: Archived
docs.text:
• Status: False
  • Class: Terminal
  • Trigger: Archive teardown is complete — all owned objects have been torn down. Set just before the teardown finalizer is removed.
  • Message: The object set is archived.
  • Re-enqueue: None (Result{}).
  • Under deadline: n/a.

docs.title: ProgressDeadlineExceeded
docs.text:
• Status: False
  • Class: Retryable (overlay)
  • Trigger: spec.progressDeadlineMinutes elapsed before the object set became ready. This is an overlay reason that relabels ObjectsNotReady or ObjectCollision — it is not a distinct code path and does not stop reconciliation. (Transient errors set no reason, so there is nothing to relabel.)
  • Message: The object set did not become ready within <N> minute(s). Last status: <original message>.
  • Re-enqueue: Inherits the re-enqueue behavior of whichever path triggered it (see each reason's "Under deadline" note above).
  • Under deadline: n/a — this is the deadline state.

docs.title: Precedence summary
docs.text:
Within a single reconcile, the checks run in this order; the first one that fires wins:

  1. MutableReferencedSecret — referenced Secrets must be immutable. (blocking; beats the deadline)
  2. ResolvedContentChanged — observed-phase digests must still match. (blocking; beats the deadline)
  3. Transient errors → Ready left unchanged, no reason (building phases, engine creation, freeing informers, establishing the watch, revision reconcile); the error is returned for backoff.
  4. ValidationFailed — revision/phase preflight validation. Like the blocking checks (1–2), this is reported via markAsNotReady and is not overridden by the deadline — a failed pre-apply check is more actionable than "deadline exceeded", so it wins.
  5. ObjectCollision — per-phase object collisions.
  6. Rollout result:
  7. complete → AllObjectsReady (True)
  8. not complete, ≥1 object progressed to a newer revision → Superseded
  9. not complete → ObjectsNotReady
  10. ProgressDeadlineExceeded overlays steps 5–6 (ObjectCollision, Superseded, ObjectsNotReady) once the deadline has passed — but not steps 1–2 or 4. Note the asymmetry within the actionable reasons: the progress deadline intentionally overrides ObjectCollision (past the deadline a collision reads as ProgressDeadlineExceeded), whereas ValidationFailed wins over it. This is a deliberate, documented choice.

The archive path (spec.lifecycleState: Archived) is separate and produces Archiving (teardown in progress), Archived (teardown complete), or a transient error reason (teardown error).

docs.title: ClusterExtension roll-up (for reference)
docs.text:
The ClusterExtension controller reads the COS Ready condition and derives its own Progressing / Installed conditions from it (progressingFromAvailable in common_controller.go). In brief:

  • MutableReferencedSecret / ResolvedContentChanged → CE Progressing=False with reason Blocked (message passed through verbatim).
  • ProgressDeadlineExceeded → CE Progressing=False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded.
  • ObjectCollision → CE Progressing=True with reason Retrying; it and ValidationFailed can drive the Installed failure reason Failed.
  • A transient error leaves COS Ready unchanged, so the CE goes neutral — it does not map to Retrying or Failed.
  • Other reasons on a not-yet-complete revision → CE Progressing=True with reason RollingOut; on a completed revision, Progressing stays Succeeded.

docs.title: Add a Catalog of Extensions to a Cluster
docs.text:
Extension authors can publish their products in catalogs. ClusterCatalogs are curated collections of Kubernetes extensions, such as Operators. Cluster administrators can add these ClusterCatalogs to their cluster. Cluster administrators can enable polling to get over-the-air updates to ClusterCatalogs when extension authors publish changes such as bug fixes and new features.

For example, the Kubernetes community Operators catalog is a catalog of curated extensions that is developed by the Kubernetes community. You can see the available extensions at Operatorhub.io. This catalog is distributed as an image quay.io/operatorhubio/catalog that can be installed on clusters.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Access to a Kubernetes cluster, for example kind, using an account with cluster-admin permissions
  • Operator Controller and Catalogd installed on the cluster
  • Kubernetes CLI (kubectl) installed on your workstation

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Create a catalog custom resource (CR):

    clustercatalog_cr.yaml
    apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterCatalog
metadata:
  name: <catalog_name>
spec:
  source:
    type: Image
    image:
      ref: <catalog_image>
      pollIntervalMinutes: <poll_interval_duration>
    catalog_image Specifies the image reference for the catalog you want to install, such as quay.io/operatorhubio/catalog:latest. poll_interval_duration Specifies the number of minutes for polling the remote registry for newer image digests. This field is optional. To disable polling, unset the field. Example `operatorhubio.yaml` CR
    apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterCatalog
metadata:
  name: operatorhubio
spec:
  source:
    type: Image
    image:
      ref: quay.io/operatorhubio/catalog:latest
      pollIntervalMinutes: 10

  2. Apply the ClusterCatalog CR:

    kubectl apply -f operatorhubio.yaml
    Example output
    clustercatalog.olm.operatorframework.io/operatorhubio created

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Run the following commands to verify the status of your catalog:

    • Check if your catalog is available on the cluster:

      kubectl get clustercatalog
      Example output
      NAME            LASTUNPACKED   SERVING   AGE
operatorhubio   18s            True      27s

    • Check the status of your catalog:

      kubectl describe clustercatalog

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Downgrading a ClusterExtension involves reverting the extension to a previously available version. This process may be necessary due to compatibility issues, unexpected behavior in the newer version, or specific feature requirements only available in an earlier release. However, downgrading carries inherent risks, such as potential data loss, issues with new CRD versions, and possible breakage of clients that rely on the newer version. Users should carefully consider these risks and be confident in their decision to proceed with the downgrade. This guide provides step-by-step instructions for performing a downgrade, including overrides to bypass default constraints and disable CRD safety checks.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before initiating the downgrade process, ensure the following prerequisites are met:

  • Backup Configurations: Always back up your current configurations and data to prevent potential loss during the downgrade.
  • Access Rights: Ensure you have the necessary permissions to modify ClusterExtension resources and perform administrative tasks.
  • Version Availability: Verify that the target downgrade version is available in your catalogs.
  • Compatibility Check: Ensure that the target version is compatible with your current system and other dependencies.

docs.title: 1. Disabling the CRD Upgrade Safety Check
docs.text:
Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) ensure that the resources used by the ClusterExtension are valid and consistent. During a downgrade, the CRD Upgrade Safety check might prevent reverting to an incompatible version. Disabling the CRD Upgrade Safety check allows the downgrade to proceed without these validations.

Disable CRD Safety Check Configuration:

Add the crdUpgradeSafety field and set its enforcement to None in the ClusterExtension resource. This configuration disables CRD safety checks during the downgrade process.

Example:

apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterExtension
metadata:
  name: example-extension
spec:
  namespace: argocd
  install:
    preflight:
      crdUpgradeSafety:
        enforcement: None
  source:
    sourceType: Catalog
    catalog:
      packageName: argocd-operator
      version: 0.6.0

Command Example:

If you prefer using the command line, you can use kubectl to modify the upgrade CRD safety check configuration.

kubectl patch clusterextension example-extension --patch '{"spec":{"install":{"preflight":{"crdUpgradeSafety":{"enforcement":"None"}}}}}' --type=merge

docs.title: 2. Ignoring Catalog Provided Upgrade Constraints
docs.text:
By default, Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) enforces upgrade constraints based on semantic versioning and catalog definitions. To allow downgrades, you need to override these constraints.

Override Configuration:

Set the upgradeConstraintPolicy to SelfCertified in the ClusterExtension resource. This configuration permits downgrades, sidegrades, and any version changes without adhering to the predefined upgrade paths.

Example:

apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterExtension
metadata:
  name: example-extension
spec:
  namespace: argocd
  install:
    preflight:
      crdUpgradeSafety:
        enforcement: None
  source:
    sourceType: Catalog
    catalog:
      packageName: argocd-operator
      version: 0.6.0
      upgradeConstraintPolicy: SelfCertified

Command Example:

If you prefer using the command line, you can use kubectl to modify the upgrade constraint policy.

kubectl patch clusterextension example-extension --patch '{"spec":{"source": {"catalog":{"upgradeConstraintPolicy":"SelfCertified"}}}}' --type=merge

docs.title: 3. Executing the Downgrade
docs.text:
Once the CRD safety checks are disabled and upgrade constraints are set, you can proceed with the actual downgrade.

  1. Edit the ClusterExtension Resource:

    Modify the ClusterExtension custom resource to specify the target version and adjust the upgrade constraints.

    kubectl edit clusterextension example-extension

  2. Update the Version:

    Within the YAML editor, update the spec section as follows:

    apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterExtension
metadata:
  name: example-extension
spec:
  namespace: argocd
  install:
    preflight:
      crdUpgradeSafety:
        enforcement: None
  source:
    sourceType: Catalog
    catalog:
      packageName: argocd-operator
      version: <target_version>
      upgradeConstraintPolicy: SelfCertified
    target_version Specify the target version you wish to downgrade to.

  3. Apply the Changes:

    Save and exit the editor. Kubernetes will apply the changes and initiate the downgrade process.

docs.title: 4. Post-Downgrade Verification
docs.text:
After completing the downgrade, verify that the ClusterExtension is functioning as expected.

Verification Steps:

  1. Check the Status of the ClusterExtension:

    kubectl get clusterextension example-extension -o yaml

    Ensure that the status reflects the target version and that there are no error messages.

  2. Validate CRD Integrity:

    Confirm that all CRDs associated with the ClusterExtension are correctly installed and compatible with the downgraded version.

    kubectl get crd | grep <extension_crd>

  3. Test Extension Functionality:

    Perform functional tests to ensure that the extension operates correctly in its downgraded state.

  4. Monitor Logs:

    Check the logs of the operator managing the ClusterExtension for any warnings or errors.

    kubectl logs deployment/<operator_deployment> -n <operator_namespace>

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: During the downgrade process, you might encounter issues. Below are common problems and their solutions:

docs.title: Downgrade Fails Due to Version Constraints
docs.text:
Solution:

  • Ensure that the upgradeConstraintPolicy is set to SelfCertified.
  • Verify that the target version exists in the catalog.
  • Check for typos or incorrect version numbers in the configuration.

docs.title: CRD Compatibility Issues
docs.text:
Solution:

  • Review the changes in CRDs between versions to ensure compatibility.
  • If disabling the CRD safety check, ensure that the downgraded version can handle the existing CRDs without conflicts.
  • Consider manually reverting CRDs if necessary, but proceed with caution to avoid data loss.

docs.title: Extension Becomes Unresponsive After Downgrade
docs.text:
Solution:

  • Restore from the backup taken before the downgrade.
  • Investigate logs for errors related to the downgraded version.
  • Verify that all dependencies required by the downgraded version are satisfied.

docs.title: Additional Resources
docs.text:
• Semantic Versioning Specification
  • Manually Verified Upgrades and Downgrades

docs.title: Explore Available Content
docs.text: After you add a catalog of extensions to your cluster, you must port forward your catalog as a service. Then you can query the catalog by using curl commands and the jq CLI tool to find extensions to install.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You have added a ClusterCatalog of extensions, such as OperatorHub.io, to your cluster.
  • You have installed the jq CLI tool.

Note

By default, Catalogd is installed with TLS enabled for the catalog webserver. The following examples will show this default behavior, but for simplicity's sake will ignore TLS verification in the curl commands using the -k flag.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Port forward the catalog server service:

    kubectl -n olmv1-system port-forward svc/catalogd-service 8443:443

  2. Return a list of all the extensions in a catalog via the v1 API endpoint: 

    curl -k https://localhost:8443/catalogs/operatorhubio/api/v1/all | jq -s '.[] | select(.schema == "olm.package") | .name'

docs.title: Install an Extension from a Catalog
docs.text: In Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) 1.0, Kubernetes extensions are scoped to the cluster. After you add a catalog to your cluster, you can install an extension by creating a custom resource (CR) and applying it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A catalog that is being served
  • The name, and optionally version, or channel, of the supported extension to be installed
  • An existing namespace in which to install the extension

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Create a CR for the Kubernetes extension you want to install:

    Example CR
    apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterExtension
metadata:
  name: <extension_name>
spec:
  namespace: <namespace_name>
  source:
    sourceType: Catalog
    catalog:
      packageName: <package_name>
      channels: [<channel1>, <channel2>]
      version: "<version>"
    extension_name Specifies a custom name for the Kubernetes extension you want to install, such as my-camel-k. package_name Specifies the name of the package you want to install, such as camel-k. channels Optional: Specifies a set of the extension's channels from which to select, such as stable or fast. version Optional: Specifies the version or version range you want installed, such as 1.3.1 or "<2". If you use a comparison string to define a version range, the string must be surrounded by double quotes ("). namespace_name Specifies a name for the namespace in which the bundle of content for the package referenced in the packageName field will be applied.

    Warning

    Currently, the following limitations affect the installation of extensions:

    • If multiple catalogs are added to a cluster, you cannot specify a catalog when you install an extension.
    • OLM 1.0 requires that all of the extensions have unique bundle and package names for dependency resolution.

    As a result, if two catalogs have an extension with the same name, the installation might fail or lead to an unintended outcome. For example, the first extension that matches might install successfully and finish without searching for a match in the second catalog.

  2. Apply the CR to the cluster:

    kubectl apply -f <cr_name>.yaml

    Success

    Example output
    clusterextension.olm.operatorframework.io/argocd created

docs.title: Uninstall an extension
docs.text: You can uninstall a Kubernetes extension and its associated custom resource definitions (CRD) by deleting the extension's custom resource (CR).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • You have an extension installed.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
• Delete the extension's CR:

    kubectl delete clusterextensions <extension_name>
    extension_name Specifies the name defined in the metadata.name field of the extension's CR. Example output
    clusterextension.olm.operatorframework.io "argocd" deleted

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Verify that the Kubernetes extension is deleted:

    kubectl get clusterextension.olm.operatorframework.io
    Example output
    No resources found

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: • Remove the extension namespace (if applicable).

docs.title: Upgrade an Extension
docs.text:
Existing extensions can be upgraded by updating the version field in the ClusterExtension resource.

For information on downgrading an extension, see Downgrade an Extension.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You have a ClusterExtension installed
  • The target version is compatible with OLM v1 (see OLM v1 limitations)
  • Any changes to the CustomResourceDefinition in the new version meet compatibility requirements (see CRD upgrade safety)
  • You are not attempting to upgrade between minor versions with a major version of zero (see Upgrades within the major version zero)

For more detailed information see Upgrade Support.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
For this example, we will be using v0.2.0 of the ArgoCD operator. If you would like to follow along with this tutorial, you can apply the following manifest to your cluster by, for example, saving it to a local file and then running kubectl apply -f FILENAME:

ArgoCD v0.2.0 manifests 
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: argocd
---
apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterExtension
metadata:
  name: argocd
spec:
  namespace: argocd
  source:
    sourceType: Catalog
    catalog:
      packageName: argocd-operator
      version: 0.2.0

If we view the current state of our ClusterExtension we should see that we have installed version 0.2.0:

kubectl get clusterextension argocd -o jsonpath-as-json="{.status.install}"

Command output

[
    {
        "bundle": {
            "name": "argocd-operator.v0.2.0",
            "version": "0.2.0"
        }
    }
]

  • To initiate our upgrade, let's update the version field in the ClusterExtension resource:

    Method 1: apply a new ClusterExtension manifest
    kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: olm.operatorframework.io/v1
kind: ClusterExtension
metadata:
  name: argocd
spec:
  namespace: argocd
  source:
    sourceType: Catalog
    catalog:
      packageName: argocd-operator
      version: 0.2.1 # Update to version 0.2.1
EOF

    Method 1 output

    clusterextension.olm.operatorframework.io/argocd configured

    Alternatively, you can use kubectl patch to update the version field:

    Method 2: run patch command
    kubectl patch clusterextension argocd --type='merge' -p '{"spec": {"source": {"catalog": {"version": "0.2.1"}}}}'

    Method 2 output

    clusterextension.olm.operatorframework.io/argocd patched

  • We can now verify that the ClusterExtension is updated to the new version:

    Get the current ClusterExtension version
    kubectl get clusterextension argocd -o jsonpath-as-json="{.status.install}"

    Updated ClusterExtension version

    [
    {
        "bundle": {
            "name": "argocd-operator.v0.2.1",
            "version": "0.2.1"
        }
    }
]

Note on the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation

After your upgrade, the contents of the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation field will differ depending on your method of upgrade. If you apply a new ClusterExtension manifest as in the first method shown, the last applied configuration will show the new version since we replaced the existing manifest. If you use the patch method or kubectl edit clusterextension, then the last applied configuration will show the old version.
